item.title: Chiricahua National Park Becomes 64th U.S. National Park After Six-Year Gap
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler, Backpacker Magazine
The United States added its 64th national park in nearly six years with the designation of Chiricahua National Monument in southeastern Arizona on October 20, 2026, following the signing of the Chiricahua National Park Act by President Trump. Located just over an hour from the Arizona-New Mexico border, the park is known as the 'Wonderland of Rocks' for its striking volcanic formations, shaped by a massive eruption about 27 million years ago. This marks the first new national park designation since West Virginia's New River Gorge National Park & Preserve in 2020. Chiricahua joins three other Arizona national parks—Grand Canyon, Petrified Forest, and Saguaro—creating a cluster of protected landscapes in the state. The park's designation comes after decades of advocacy, as it was originally established as a national monument in 1924. While the physical protections remain largely unchanged, the new status is expected to boost tourism and economic activity, as seen in similar parks like White Sands National Park, which saw increased visitation after its 2019 designation. Visitors can explore over 17 miles of hiking trails, including the Bonita Canyon Scenic Drive, while also experiencing the park's rich cultural history as the ancestral home of the Chiricahua Apache. The area's unique 'sky island' location between the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts supports diverse ecosystems, with over 200 bird species, 70 mammals, 46 reptiles, and 8 amphibians. Backpacking is not permitted within the park, but dayhikes range from easy to strenuous, with popular routes like the Echo Canyon Loop, Natural Bridge, and the longer Big Loop Hike offering dramatic views of the volcanic rock formations. The park's international dark sky status and historic sites, such as the Faraway Ranch district, further enhance its appeal. While entry and parking remain free, the increased attention from national park status is anticipated to bring more visitors and economic benefits to the region.

item.title: Bilt transfer partners: How to maximize your points with airlines and hotels
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Bilt transfer partners: How to maximize your points with airlines and hotels Bilt offers several ways to redeem Bilt Points, but transferring them to airline and hotel loyalty programs can be one of the most valuable options. With partners including United MileagePlus, Atmos Rewards and Hilton Honors, Bilt members can use their points to book everything from domestic flights to international business-class seats and luxury hotel stays. However, not all transfer partners offer the same value, and choosing the right program can make a significant difference in how far your points go. Here's everything you need to know about Bilt's transfer partners, including the available programs, transfer ratios and some of the best ways to redeem your points. Who are Bilt's transfer partners? Bilt partners with 18 airline loyalty programs, giving members plenty of options for redeeming their points for flights. You can transfer Bilt Points to the following airline programs: Bilt also partners with seven hotel loyalty programs: Additionally, Bilt Points transfer to Amtrak Guest Rewards at a 2:1 ratio. Unless otherwise noted, Bilt Points transfer to these programs at a 1:1 ratio. That means 1,000 Bilt Points generally become 1,000 airline miles or hotel points. How long do Bilt Points transfers take? Most transfers from Bilt to its partner programs are instantaneous. TPG's tests have found that Bilt Points typically arrive in partner loyalty accounts within minutes. This is important when booking award flights or hotel stays, since award availability can change quickly. However, transfer times aren't guaranteed, so it's always best to confirm availability before transferring your points. To help avoid delays, make sure the name on your Bilt account matches the name on your airline or hotel loyalty account. It's also a good idea to create and link your loyalty program accounts in advance, rather than waiting until you're ready to book an award. How do you transfer Bilt Points to partners? You can transfer Bilt Points to airline and hotel loyalty partners through the Bilt app or website. First, log in to your Bilt account, navigate to the "Rewards" tab and select "Transfer." From there, you'll see a list of available transfer partners. Select your desired airline or hotel loyalty program and link your account if you haven't already done so. Then, enter the number of Bilt Points you want to transfer and confirm the transaction. Note that there is a minimum point transfer of 2,000 Bilt Points for members who are Blue Status and a minimum point transfer of 1,000 Bilt Points for members who are Silver, Gold or Platinum Bilt Status. Additionally, all transfers must be done in 1,000-point increments. Keep in mind that Bilt transfers are irreversible, so it's best to confirm award availability and have a specific redemption in mind before transferring your points. What are the best Bilt transfer partners? The best Bilt transfer partner for you will depend on your travel plans, preferred airlines and hotels and award availability. However, some programs offer particularly valuable redemption opportunities. One standout is World of Hyatt, which uses an award chart and offers opportunities to book high-end properties for significantly fewer points than you might expect based on cash rates. Hyatt award nights start at just 3,000 points, making it a solid option for both budget-friendly and luxury stays. Keep in mind that Bilt's 1:1 transfer ratio to Hyatt will decrease to 4:3 on Jan. 1, 2027. While this will make Hyatt transfers less valuable, the program should remain a worthwhile option for Bilt members, particularly when cash rates are high. Atmos Rewards is another valuable option. The joint loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines offers access to an extensive network of airline partners, including American Airlines and other Oneworld carriers. This is a useful work-around since Bilt doesn't transfer directly to American AAdvantage. Depending on the route and award availability, you can find one-way business-class flights between the U.S. and Europe starting at 45,000 Atmos Rewards points. Other worthwhile options include Air Canada Aeroplan, which offers access to numerous Star Alliance partners, and Air France-KLM Flying Blue, which regularly offers discounted award flights through its monthly Promo Rewards. Bilt also occasionally offers transfer bonuses, particularly during its monthly Rent Day promotions. These can make certain partners even more appealing, so it's worth checking for available bonuses before transferring your points. What are Bilt points worth? TPG values Bilt Points at 2.2 cents apiece, per our October 2026 valuations. This valuation reflects the value you can potentially get by transferring points to airline and hotel loyalty programs. At that rate, 10,000 Bilt Points are worth approximately $220. However, the value you'll get depends on how you redeem your points. For example, you can redeem Bilt Points for travel through the Bilt Travel portal at 1.25 cents apiece, or put them toward a future home down payment at 1.5 cents apiece. That means 10,000 points would be worth $125 or $150, respectively. Transferring Bilt Points to airline and hotel partners can be one of the best ways to maximize their value, particularly when booking expensive flights or hotel stays. However, it's worth comparing your redemption options to determine which makes the most sense for your travel plans. How can you earn Bilt Points? You can earn Bilt Points through eligible rent and mortgage payments, everyday purchases and Bilt's network of neighborhood partners. One way to maximize your earnings is by carrying a Bilt credit card. The following three cards earn transferable Bilt Points: - Bilt Blue Card (see rates and fees): Earn 1 point per dollar spent on everyday purchases. This card has no annual fee (see rates and fees). - Bilt Obsidian Card (see rates and fees): Earn 3 points per dollar spent on either dining or groceries (on up to $25,000 in grocery purchases annually), 2 points per dollar spent on travel and 1 point per dollar spent on other eligible purchases. This card has a $95 annual fee (see rates and fees). - Bilt Palladium Card (see rates and fees): Earn 2 points per dollar spent on everyday purchases, excluding housing payments. This card has a $495 annual fee (see rates and fees). All three cards also offer opportunities to earn up to 1.25 points per dollar spent on eligible rent and mortgage payments without transaction fees, depending on your selected rewards option and everyday spending. TPG senior editorial director Summer Hull considers the Bilt Palladium Card one of her "favorite additions to her wallet in 2026", thanks to its ability to earn unlimited 2 points per dollar spent on everyday purchases and transfer those points to partners like Atmos Rewards. You don't need a Bilt credit card to earn points, though. Bilt members can also earn rewards on eligible rent payments, bookings through the Bilt Travel Portal and purchases with participating Neighborhood Benefits partners, including restaurants, fitness studios and more. To learn more, read our full review of the Bilt Blue, Bilt Obsidian and Bilt Palladium. TPG staffers have put Bilt's transfer partners to use for everything from short domestic flights to luxury hotel stays. TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak recently transferred Bilt Points to Atmos Rewards to top off her account for a one-way Alaska Airlines flight from Portland International Airport (PDX) to Spokane International Airport (GEG). She redeemed just 5,000 Atmos Rewards points plus $5.60 in taxes and fees for a flight that would have otherwise cost $184. That works out to approximately 3.6 cents per point, well above TPG's valuation of 2.2 cents per Bilt Point. Meanwhile, TPG managing editor for loyalty programs, Lyndsey Matthews, transferred Bilt Points earned with her Bilt Palladium Card to Atmos Rewards for a last-minute trip to Key West, Florida. She redeemed 12,500 Atmos Rewards points plus $18 in taxes and fees for a one-way American Airlines flight from New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA) to Key West International Airport (EYW). The flight would have cost $331 in cash, giving her a redemption value of approximately 2.5 cents per point. Finally, TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson transferred 130,000 Bilt Points to World of Hyatt to help book several hotel stays. He combined those points with existing Hyatt points and transfers from Chase Ultimate Rewards to book stays at properties including the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme. At this property, he redeemed 70,000 points for two nights that would have cost $2,900 in cash — a value of approximately 4.1 cents per point. With more than two dozen airline, hotel and rail transfer partners, Bilt members have a variety of options for using their points toward travel. However, not every transfer will offer the same value. Before moving your Bilt Points to a partner program, compare award rates with cash prices, check for available transfer bonuses and confirm that the flight or hotel you want to book is available. Since transfers are irreversible, it's generally best to have a specific redemption in mind before moving your points.

item.title: Canada's ghost island where guests still check in
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
No cars, no phone signal: Canada's ghost island where guests still check in Once the thriving heart of Labrador's fishing industry, Battle Harbour has found new life as an island retreat with barely a trace of modern life. Several livyers have gathered on the wharf. Sleeves rolled up, four fishermen who "live here" on this remote Labrador island are splitting cod. Behind them, suit-clad merchants and more fishers, some in waterproof oilskins, have arranged themselves for a group photo against a white clapboard building with ochre-red trim. But our ferry approaches the wharf, something seems off. Everyone's as grey as the sky and nobody is moving. I give my head a shake and remember that I'm arriving at a place that proudly describes itself as "nine miles from normal". So, while these fellows were alive in around 1900, when this was the saltfish capital of the world, they've since been plucked from archival photos and turned into life-sized cardboard cutouts. "Welcome to Battle Harbour," says Peter Bull, the executive director of the Battle Harbour Historic Trust, as we scramble off the ferry on a wooden plank. Bull quickly runs through the practicalities. Lunch is in half an hour at 12:30. A tour starts at 13:30. An Arctic fox family lives in the old cemetery. Two historic wireless radio towers need to be saved. There's no mobile phone service and just one communal Wi-Fi spot. Sunrise comes at 06:19. Wanda Fifield will walk me to my room. "This [is the] emergency system – you just turn this button on," Fifield says, stopping at a walkie talkie in the hallway near my room. "If there's a problem in the nighttime, if you're sick or hurt or anything, just press this square button. You tell them your problem. You tell them that you're staying at the Merchant Building because they'll need to know what cottage to go to." With restored wooden houses, weathered fishing stages where catches were once processed and 16 private summer residences, Battle Harbour looks remarkably well preserved. But it has been more than half a century since anyone lived here year-round, and even longer since it was the unofficial capital of Labrador. I've got two nights to step back in time. Getting to Battle Harbour is an adventure in itself. First, you fly to the delightfully named Happy Valley-Goose Bay in mainland Labrador, then drive for five hours along the forest-flanked Expedition 51° highway, hoping to spot a moose and yearning for an outhouse. There are no services for most of the journey. From the wharf in Mary's Harbour, you then catch the daily passenger "ferry" for guests – a lofty name for a boat so small your luggage may be stacked in the bathroom. Plan your trip: When to visit: Battle Harbour is only open from June to early September. Confirm seasonal dates before booking. Getting there: Fly to Happy Valley-Goose Bay, then drive five hours to Mary's Harbour. A passenger ferry (for overnight guests only) departs at 11:00 each day and returns at 09:00 each morning. The journey takes 60 to 75 minutes. Staying overnight: Accommodation is in restored cottages and historic inn rooms. Two-night packages start at C$1,570 (£835; $1,106) for two people, including accommodation, return ferry transfers, meals and a guided historical tour. Taxes and gratuities are extra. Day trips: Separate day trips are also available during the summer season. Check with the operator for current schedules and prices. For 14.5km (9 miles), the boat winds past craggy coastline and near-shore islands, which look otherworldly if it's foggy and desolate if it's grey. Gulls, kittiwakes and gannets may soar alongside the boat and sometimes you'll spot icebergs, humpback whales and minkes. When Battle Island's buildings finally come into view, it's hard to believe that this tiny, half-mile long island was once teeming with fishermen and merchants. In the 1770s, English merchant John Slade established a trading operation on this tiny island that became a gateway to Labrador's rich fishing grounds. Salt cod was processed here and exported to Europe, the Caribbean and beyond. At its peak, there was a hospital, school, church and wireless station, and a permanent population of around 300. Thousands more seasonal fishermen passed through, including floaters who lived on schooners and stationers who built temporary shacks on land. But Battle Harbour's fortunes eventually faded. A devastating fire in 1930, declining fish stocks and a provincial resettlement programme in the 1960s gradually emptied the island. By the 1970s, its last year-round residents had gone. The final blow to the island came on 2 July 1992, when the federal government's cod moratorium closed the fishery and instantly threw 30,000 people across Newfoundland and Labrador out of work. Today, Battle Harbour feels like a ghost island, its restored buildings preserving a world that has all but vanished. Run by a trust, the car-free historic site is only open to guests for around three months each summer, but for those that know it best, the island is anything but forgotten. Bull's connection to Battle Harbour stretches back more than a century, to when his grandfather fished along the Labrador coast. He has worked here since 2013, living on the island for most of the summer and returning to his home in St John's each September with enough cod, squid, mackerel and berries like bakeapple and partridgeberry to get him through winter. "When I die, my ashes are going to spread out where I pick partridgeberries," he confides, "and I'm going to come back as a partridgeberry." Nelson Smith has his own life-long connection to Battle Harbour. He helped restore its historic buildings and has been leading tours here for nearly three decades. "Every building is going to smell different because of the different stuff stored in them," Smith promises in his thick Labradorian accent. "If you hears me say a word you don't understand, stop me and I'll try to explain it to you." In Newfoundland English, this cluster of musty buildings is called "the rooms", with individual "stores" named for what they once held. The Pork Store smells faintly of molasses, while the Salt Store contains the mineral still used to preserve cod. The tour continues past more life-like cutouts: a dapper merchant, a young fisherman standing in a wooden boat, an older fisherman sitting by a cod trap. "The best way I likes my saltfish is two years old," Smith offers, explaining how cod was cleaned, salted and dried on raised, open-air wooden platforms known as flakes. In the Salt Store's loft, I stand where American polar explorer Robert E Peary presided over two 1909 press conferences and claimed he had reached the North Pole. He transmitted his first expedition account from the nearby Marconi station to the New York Times. Visitors can even stay overnight in some of these historic structures. I'm staying in the Merchant Building's Harry Smith Room, named after an employee of the island's former general store. There are also five restored cottages and 12 other ensuite rooms. A quilt covers my wooden bed and a space heater fights the chill that lingers in the old building, despite its restoration. There's no television, and the only sound is the quiet. Settling into a swivel armchair, I face the sea as I leaf through the guestbook. "Best view on the island. The iceberg was framed by our window." "Something you have to experience rather than explain." "So much serenity." At dinner – Labrador char, pan-fried cod and moose pot pie, served at communal dining tables – there's talk of Northern Lights, so I spend a restless first night peering out the window and stepping out onto the wrap-around deck. I have better luck at sunrise when I follow a dirt path to the old cemetery to see foxes emerge from their den on a rocky hillside. From the cemetery, I take the Battle Harbour Footpath for a 1.9km (1.2-mile) stroll past a newer cemetery and a memorial for three men killed in a 1976 seaplane crash. Two local boys stumbled upon the wreckage, some of which is still here. One of them was Smith. Towards the end of the footpath, I see the Marconi towers, the last surviving pair of their kind in North America. Built in 1906 and rebuilt in 1931 using a radio wave-based wireless telegraph system created by Italy's Guglielmo Marconi, they once guided mariners and transmitted messages. "They're pretty special and they're an important part of the skyline here," says Bull. The trust is trying to raise C$200,000 (£106,000/$140,000) to repair them. Strong winds scupper my plans to go cod fishing, but I manage a short boat trip to Cape St Charles to stand at the most easterly point in continental North America. Then I zip across the tickle (channel) to hike Great Caribou Island, where I find Tanya Russell, a local postmistress and amateur photographer, in a blueberry patch. Russell tells me that she loves "the quiet, the water, the saltwater air, the birds, the foxes – just everything at Battle Harbour. And you gets to meet a lot of wonderful people." At my final breakfast, it's time to say goodbye to fellow guests and life-size cutouts alike. I'm eating near a cutout made from an iconic black-and-white photograph shot at Battle Harbour more than a century ago: a sombre boy flanked by two enormous cod. This boy, Victor Croucher, is buried on the island, but here in the dining hall he's another ghostly presence in a place that stubbornly refuses to die. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Marriott opening yet another safari camp in Tanzania’s Serengeti
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Marriott opening yet another safari camp in Tanzania’s Serengeti Marriott is planning to open its latest safari camp in Tanzania's Serengeti, and it looks like a stunner. Mereshi Safari Camp Serengeti, Autograph Collection will open in November, just a short drive from the Fort Ikoma airstrip in Tanzania's Serengeti National Park (your guide will be there to meet you with bottled water and chilled, scented towels). The camp is located on the traditional land of the Ikoma people and guests will be able to take advantage of daily game drives into the park to see its incredible wildlife. The camp will have a total of 18 tented suites, each of which will comprise 775 square feet of indoor and outdoor space. Constructed of timber, stone and canvas, the tents are decorated with natural materials and traditional crafts including greenwood furniture and locally-sourced woven textiles and will feature east-facing private decks for prime sunrise views. Guests should also enjoy sumptuous beds and bracing outdoor showers. Designed by the Arusha, Tanzania-based firm Dunia Designs (they also did Mapito Safari Camp Serengeti, Autograph Collection), the main lodge was inspired by indigenous acacia trees and will feature a bar and shared lounging and dining spaces. There will also be a private boma, or enclosed dining area, nearby, for firelit sundowners and dinners under the stars, and a deck overlooking a water feature as well as a small spa, a pool and fitness center and a curio shop for souvenirs. The lodge's main restaurant, Mila, will be an indoor-outdoor space to keep guests connected with nature. It will serve breakfast after morning drives, family-style lunches and leisurely dinners after the dusk game drive. Speaking of game drives, two shared game drives and guided walks per day along with refreshments are included in nightly rates, as are all meals, select alcoholic and nonalcoholic beverages, return transfers from either the Fort Ikoma or Seronera airstrips, a traditional boma dining experience and complimentary laundry and Wi-Fi. Marriott's site lists the hotel as opening in November 2027, but bookings are currently open for Jan. 4, 2027, onward. Nightly rates start at $1,967 based on double occupancy, but award redemption rates are not yet published. That said, nightly award redemptions start at around 190,000 for its sister property, Mapito, so expect rates to fall in line with that. From Jan. 4 through Mar. 27, the lodge is offering an opening rate special where you can earn 25,000 bonus Marriott Bonvoy points on eligible bookings using the following code: S2449. Marriott first got into the safari sector back in 2023 when it opened the JW Marriott Masai Mara Lodge. Since then it has opened a handful of other camps including the Ritz-Carlton, Masai Mara, Kinara, A Luxury Collection Safari Camp, Masai Mara in Kenya (formerly the Mara Eden Safari Camp), Mapito Safari Camp and, most recently, the JW Marriott Mount Kenya Rhino Reserve Safari Camp, which was one of the most anticipated hotel openings of 2026. Hopefully the other major chains will start getting into the game, so to speak, and it'll be easier than ever to redeem points for incredible wildlife experiences. If you end up booking Mereshi, leave us a comment and let us know how it is!

item.title: Japan is Making it Harder for Non-Citizens to Become Permanent Residents
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Tourists from around the world continue to flock to Japanâs bustling megacities and quiet onsen towns, generating a record-setting (and sometimes unmanageable) influx of travelers: an increase from 25.1 million in 2023 to 42.7 million in 2025, according to the countryâs tourism board. In the face of this boom, Japan is setting more boundaries with visitors, including levying an increased tourist tax and, as of October 1, making it harder for non-citizens to obtain residence status. The number of foreign residents in Japan reached a record 3.96 million people in June 2025, prompting Japanâs immigration agency to tighten its eligibility guidelines for the country's permanent residency permit, which is available to foreign workers who have continuously lived in Japan for at least 10 years. The new rules are just one part of a larger framework of policies adopted by the Japanese government on January 23, 2026 called the âComprehensive Measures for the Acceptance and Orderly Coexistence of Foreign Nationals.â The government says the policies are designed to address âanxieties and feelings of unfairness felt by some citizens as the number of foreign residents increases,â Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi wrote in a September 26 post on X. That means applicants to Japan's foreign residence permit will soon face stricter language proficiency requirements, more expensive fees, and a higher income threshold. If you're pursuing permanent residency or a long-term stay in Japan, here's what you need to know. What is changing? The new requirements dictate that applicants must earn more than the average Japanese household income (which was about $36,350 per year in 2024, according to a survey by the countryâs health, labor, and welfare ministry). In addition, applicants must now show pension benefits that match what they would have received after 30 years in the countryâs employee pension program. (If the applicant falls short on the pension requirement, the guidelines say they can supplement with additional âfinancial assets," but does not provide specifics beyond that.) The government also announced a dramatic 20-fold hike in the application fee, which is now 20,000 yen, or about $1,260. That said, the cost is still relatively affordable compared to permanent residency-related applications in countries like the UK, which cost 3,226 British pounds (about $4,261), and the US, which can cost upwards of $10,000, according to Arton. Qualifying for Japan's permanent residency visa isn't just about financial eligibility. Applicants will also need a proficient understanding of the Japanese language, which the guidelines define as at or above a B1 level on the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test; however, itâs not yet clear how applicants will be asked to demonstrate their language ability. The income changes will retroactively affect applications filed from April 2026. Other changes, such as the pension requirement, will be implemented starting April 1, 2027. âFor Americans thinking of making Japan their long-term home, the message is clear: financial security alone is no longer enough,â Armand Arton, CEO of citizenship firm Arton Capital, tells CondÃ© Nast Traveler. âApplicants must also demonstrate a genuine commitment to living and working in the country, as well as integrating into Japanese society.â Who is eligible for Japanâs permanent residency permit? To apply, you need to have lived in Japan for 10 continuous years, with at least five of those years under a work or residence visa. If youâve been out of the country for more than six consecutive months without a âreasonableâ justification, or for a total of two-and-a-half years over the decade, your application could receive ânegativeâ marks. That said, there are exceptions to the 10-year rule: For example, if youâve been deemed a âhighly skilled foreign professionalâ or if youâve been married to a Japanese resident for at least five years (and your spouse has lived in the country for at least three continuous years). Japan doesnât want new residents who will bounce in and out of the country, but rather those who will commit to building a life locally: âItâs offering quality of life and cultural immersion, rather than passport power and access,â says Arton. If you meet these payment, income, language, and residency requirements, you can submit your application to a local immigration office in Japan. Applicants should prepare documents such as a copy of your health insurance card and proof that youâve paid your resident taxes on time (through means such as providing a copy of your bank passbook) After everything has been submitted, expect a four-to-six-month processing timeline (all form and application details are available at Japanâs immigration agency website). Interested in moving to Japan? Here are your other options If you donât meet the requirements for a permanent residency permit, Japan offers several temporary relocation pathways. If youâre deemed a âhighly skilled professionalâ who will drive the local economy and academic research, you could get a five-year highly skilled professional residence visa. If you work as an entertainer, a chef specializing in an international cuisine, or in one of the other qualifying industries, you could apply for a working visa, which lasts between three months and five years. (You can check whether you qualify for the highly skilled professional or work visa by checking the evaluation guidelines on Japanâs immigration services website.) If you have Japanese ancestry, consider applying for a long-term resident visa, which grants you between six months and five years in the country. Or, if you work remotely and want to stay in Japan for six months, the digital nomad visa may be the best fit. A comprehensive list of all of Japanâs visas is available on its foreign affairs ministry website.

item.title: A new sleeper train is coming to Europe in spring 2027 – and it's actually affordable
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Sleeper trains are getting a lot of love as of late. As they should â there's nothing quite like falling asleep in one city and waking up in the next with the gentle hum of a train ticking along the tracks. If you've been tempted by Europe's sleeper trains, but have found the prices a little scary, or the idea of sharing a cabin with a stranger on one of the more affordable trains slightly less appealing â we have some good news. A new company is promising to redefine short-haul travel. Berlin start-up Nox Mobility is entering the train game with their first sleeper train service departing tracks from 23 March 2027. The new trains promise âgood sleep, private rooms onlyâ and will start with their first route from Hamburg and Munich, with stops in Bremen and Augsburg. Starting at 65 euros (approximately Â£55) for one-way fares, every passenger gets a âNox Suiteâ. That means your own private space with sliding doors. In each suite you'll find large lie-flat seats, a table to work or eat at, room for lots of luggage, and power outlets within reach. A later roll-out set for 2029 promises even more space with fully private rooms designed for one or two passengers, though bathrooms are still shared. Travelling with the family? Kids under four years old can travel for free with an adult passenger. âTaking a night train in Europe still means sharing a cabin with four strangers and hoping the ride turns out to be bearable. With Nox, every passenger has their own space to work and rest in," says Thibault Constant, Co-Founder of Nox Mobility whose âSimply Railwayâ YouTube has a 300,000-strong following and who has travelled on more than 400 night trains. "A night on a Nox train should eventually bring together everything that used to take three bookings: getting there, staying the night and the morning at the destination. This is how we put hospitality in motion. The train is the heart of it, but only the beginning.â He founded the company with Janek Smalla, who led the operational launch of FlixTrain â so passengers know they'll be in good hands. Trains depart Hamburg at approximately 9pm and arrive in Munich at around 8am the following morning. A key feature on this route is that the train doesn't stop-start throughout the night too â meaning you'll have a more restful sleep. The plan is to launch first services by 2027, but by 2035 Nox aims to serve more than 100 European cities including Stockholm, Copenhagen, Amsterdam, Paris, Rome and Barcelona.

item.title: Where was The Diplomat filmed? Inside the political thriller's season 4 locations
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Diplomat filmed? This story contains major spoilers for season four. Watching The Diplomat is like being a fly on the wall in some of the world’s most powerful rooms and buildings. But the Netflix series, though often immensely dramatic, rarely puts its characters in places that reflect them intimately. Instead, as production designer Curt Beech explains, The Diplomat is about “bringing the characters together physically but never emotionally in spaces the public don’t get to see.” “The places may be historical, but they're almost never personal,” he says. “That is what's so different about this show from a design standpoint. Usually, we're creating someone's bedroom or their house, and we dig into their family history and who they are and what they like. We don't get any of that here because the spaces that they inhabit are not theirs. They are almost always visitors.” The fourth season of The Diplomat opens with a bang, literally. In the first episode, US President Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, survives an assassination attempt outside Windsor Castle. She becomes increasingly unpredictable afterwards, confusing her husband Todd (Bradley Whitford), Vice President Hal Wyler (Rufus Sewell), and Kate Wyler, the US ambassador to the UK (Keri Russell). The story brings the characters from Windsor Castle to Washington, DC to Lucca, Italy, where it concludes on a cliffhanger at a meeting of the G7. Beech used some of the same locations and sets from past seasons, but also brought new locations to life in England, New York, and Italy. The interior sets were created at Steiner Studios in New York, while Wrotham House returned as Winfield House, the residence of the United States ambassador in London. Here Beech breaks down the key locations from The Diplomat Season 4. Season 4 opens with an impromptu visit to Windsor Castle. As the envoy leaves the British royal residence to fly back to the US, President Penn gets shot by an unknown assailant. Beech combined nine different locations to create Windsor Castle and its grounds. The exterior and inner courtyard were filmed at Burghley House, while Belvoir Castle, Lancaster House and the British Foreign Office were used for interiors. Back in the US, the team filmed at Woolworth Estate, St. Josaphat Monastery Library and Sleepy Hollow Country Club. The grandiose panic room where Kate and Hal are locked down after the shooting was filmed in the crypt of a church on the Upper West Side. “It's a lot of different architectural styles, but that is typical of these houses,” Beech says. “Windsor has a bunch of things going on because these houses are very, very old, and they've been built during different centuries with different people in charge of the construction. We embraced that. We also have a mix of things that are accurate to Windsor Castle and things that aren’t.” After she is shot, President Penn is airlifted in Marine One to a docked United States aircraft carrier for surgery. Beech used the parking lot at Steiner Studios for the helicopter landing, while a Marine training facility in New York City was transformed into the interiors. “We did real takeoffs and landings with the helicopter,” Beech says. “While it was on the ground, we dressed the interior because Marine One feels like a private jet inside. It's very luxurious and well appointed. But you can’t add weight to a helicopter like that without going through a lot of different FAA approvals, so we couldn’t keep it dressed while flying.” As in the past, Winfield House’s exterior was filmed Wrotham Park, an estate in Hertfordshire. Some of the interiors were built at Steiner, while others were filmed inside Wrotham Park. “There's a blue room, a library, and a red room in the real building,” Beech says. “The foyer is also there. The green room, the Wedgewood hallway, and the blue study are on stage in New York. It takes a lot of coordination to keep track. The actors are incredible because they're able to tap back into whatever they were doing at that moment two months ago, and make it feel like they just turned the corner and are walking into a room.” The US Embassy in London’s Nine Elms was built on a soundstage in London for earlier seasons. The set was shipped to Steiner for Season 3 and rebuilt there. In Season 4, not much has changed. “We moved some furniture around to get better lighting, but nothing major has changed in those spaces,” Beech says. The production did shoot one scene, a meeting between CIA station chief Eidra Park (Ali Ahn) and deputy chief Stuart Hayford (Ato Essandoh), in Nine Elms. “That was right around the corner from the embassy, which was incredible to see,” Beech says. “That building is in so many different shows now and it’s beautiful.” Eidra’s modern apartment, where Stuart eventually moves in as they begin a relationship, was a real apartment in Tribeca. “This is another space that's personal, but not,” Beech says. “We told the story that she moves a lot for the safety of her position. She’s never in the same place for very long. So it’s very stark and doesn’t have a lot of personality.” For Season 4, Beech made some alterations to the White House set. He decided not to use the Oval Office seen in prior seasons and to shift the action into President Penn’s private study. “The president typically does have a study, and it's right off the Oval Office, but it’s very small,” Beech says. “You see lots of pictures of Obama sitting in his. We made a very large study for her that has three separate zones – a work zone, a meeting zone, and a power zone where her desk is. That does not exist in the real White House, but it does in our White House.” In one scene, Todd is swimming laps in the White House pool. That also doesn’t exist in real life. The scene was filmed in the basement of the Woolworth Building in Tribeca. “There used to be a pool years and years ago in the White House,” Beech says. “They plastered it over, and it's now the press briefing room. But you see in the old pictures there was a really beautiful room with arched windows and that’s where the pool was.” Although 10 Downing Street has appeared in previous seasons, the set this year was new. “That was filmed at a location in the UK that was no longer available, so we built it on our stage,” Beech says. “We also used the Steinway Mansion in New York for the building’s iconic stairs.” When a new prime minister comes into power midway through the season, viewers might notice subtle shifts in the décor. “It got a bit more sparse, indicating that she had just gotten there,” Beech says. “They had moved him out; she hadn't completely moved in yet. So some pictures are off the walls, and the lamp on his desk changed. It's small stuff.” The exterior of 10 Downing Street was filmed outside the British Foreign Office in London. “We wound up building the doorway and the lectern in a parking lot in Brooklyn with a green screen, and then we added it together with what we shot in London on that street,” Beech explains. Kate goes to meet with the newly-minted British prime minister in the family home of the prime minister’s husband, offering a rare glimpse into a character’s private life. Beech used two different locations to create the vast manor house. The entry and gate were shot at Ingatestone Hall in Essex, and the interior was filmed in a house on Long Island. “In England with these huge estates, it's very expensive to keep them going, so the family compresses to living in one wing of the house,” Beech says. “We wanted to tell that story about her house, and there’s a coldness to it. Her office space is in a room that is gigantic for an office. And there are heaters everywhere.” The season concludes with a tumultuous visit to Lucca, Italy, where the members of the G7 are holding a summit. The production went to Lucca for six weeks to film in eight different locations. These included Villa Viesca, the former summer home of Salvatore and Wanda Ferragamo, and Dimora Ghirlandaio, a resort in Tuscany, both of which comprised the villas where the American envoy stays during the summit. The G7 meetings were held at the recently restored Villa Reale di Marlia, Villa Medici in Poggio a Caiano, and Villa Medicea La Petraia. “We were going play Florence for Lucca, but we leaned into Lucca as Lucca, and it felt better and more authentic,” Beech says. “We went to the Pitti Palace in Florence and determined that it wasn't right. Most of the time, the vibe is very modern in these meetings. We decided to make it very classical. We embraced the vibe of this incredible room with floor-to-ceiling frescoes, and we built custom desks that had little fresco elements that matched the walls. These meetings are very bespoke, so everything is always created for them. We did that, but in a slightly different manner.”

item.title: Are Your Backpacking Meals Providing Enough Fuel? Check These 5 Numbers
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy You’re standing in front of a display of backpacking meals at your local outdoor store, deciding what to eat on your next trip. Chicken Alfredo sounds good. So does mushroom risotto. Maybe you’ll try lasagna for the third night. You toss a few pouches into your cart. After all, they’re designed for backpackers, so they should provide the fuel you need. Right? But flip those packages over, and you’ll find some surprisingly large differences. Two meals that sound equally satisfying might provide vastly different amounts of calories, carbohydrates, protein, and sodium. And unless you check those numbers, you won’t know whether your dinner fits your nutritional needs. As a registered dietitian and ultralight backpacker, I pay close attention to these numbers when developing recipes. The same principles apply whether you’re purchasing commercial meals or making your own. To illustrate, I compared three commercially packaged dinners with two of my DIY recipes. As you can see, not all backpacking meals are going to give you the same nutrients. All values represent the entire pouch or one complete DIY recipe serving, not the manufacturer’s suggested individual serving for multi-serving pouches. Calories per ounce are based on dry food weight before adding water. Nutrition values are from the provided product labels and DIY recipe calculations. Serving sizes can be misleading, especially when you’re burning thousands of calories hiking. Mountain House Beef Lasagna and Peak Refuel Chicken Alfredo both contain two servings per pouch, but the Alfredo contains nearly twice as many calories. Good To-Go’s Mushroom Risotto contains 410 calories in its single-serving pouch. That’s a substantial difference between three dinners you might choose simply because they sound good. If you don’t check the labels, you could end up carrying far fewer calories than you need. I always look at the calories in the portion I plan to eat rather than relying on suggested serving sizes. The same applies to homemade meals. A recipe that claims to feed two people might not provide enough fuel for two hungry backpackers. How much you need at dinner depends on your daily energy requirements and what you’ve already eaten, not the number of servings printed on the package. When you’re carrying several days of food, every ounce matters. That’s why I calculate calorie density by dividing a meal’s total calories by its dry weight in ounces. The five meals in the table range from approximately 120 to 168 calories per ounce. That difference can add up over a weeklong trip, especially if you’re struggling to carry enough calories without adding excessive pack weight. Fat contains 9 calories per gram, compared with 4 for carbohydrates and protein, so meals containing more fat tend to provide more calories per ounce. When developing my own recipes, I use ingredients like nuts, oils, and full-fat dairy powders to increase calorie density without adding much weight or volume. But I don’t simply maximize fat, either. My goal is to provide enough carbohydrates to fuel hiking and enough protein to support recovery, then use calorie-dense ingredients to help meet energy needs without making the meal unnecessarily bulky. It’s easy to focus on calories and protein when comparing backpacking meals, but carbohydrates are especially important for fueling your miles. Your body stores carbohydrates as glycogen in your muscles and liver, providing an important energy source during hiking, especially when you’re climbing steep terrain or pushing the pace. Sports nutrition guidelines recommend approximately 5 to 7 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of body weight daily for moderate exercise, with higher amounts for more demanding activity. For a 150-pound hiker, that’s roughly 340 to 475 grams per day, spread across meals and snacks. Peak Refuel’s Chicken Alfredo provides 46 grams of carbohydrates, while Mountain House Beef Lasagna contains 60 grams. Despite providing nearly twice the calories of the lasagna, the Alfredo contains fewer carbohydrates. That doesn’t automatically make the lasagna a better choice, nor does a dinner containing 100 grams of carbohydrates necessarily provide better fuel. I consider how each meal contributes to my daily carbohydrate needs and account for any differences elsewhere in my menu. I also check fiber, since large amounts can cause digestive discomfort for some hikers during strenuous activity. Protein helps repair and rebuild muscle tissue after exercise, especially when you’re hiking long distances on consecutive days. Endurance athletes generally benefit from approximately 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily. Sports nutrition research also suggests that approximately 20 to 40 grams of high-quality protein per meal can effectively stimulate muscle protein synthesis, although individual needs vary. The meals listed above display a wide range of protein content, but remember that more is not always better. More protein in one sitting doesn’t necessarily translate into greater muscle recovery; a low-protein dinner can still fit into a menu that provides adequate protein throughout the day. When developing recipes, I consider protein alongside carbohydrates, fat, and total calories rather than trying to pack as much protein as possible into every serving. At home, we’re often encouraged to limit sodium. On trail, the picture is more complicated because we lose sodium through sweat, and those losses vary with temperature, exertion, and individual sweat composition. Mountain House Beef Lasagna contains 1,180 milligrams of sodium per pouch, while my Basil Walnut Ziti provides just 324 milligrams. That’s a substantial difference, but it doesn’t automatically mean one is better for every hiker. I track sodium when developing recipes, so I know how much each meal contributes to my overall intake, including salty snacks and electrolyte drinks. A higher-sodium dinner might fit my needs on a hot, strenuous day, but I wouldn’t assume it replaces everything lost through sweat. I consider sodium alongside my overall hydration and fueling plan rather than automatically choosing the meal with the lowest number. So, how do you choose the right backpacking dinner? More calories, carbohydrates, or protein don’t automatically make one meal better than another. I look for a balance of carbohydrates to fuel hiking, protein to support recovery, and calorie-dense fats to help meet my energy needs without adding unnecessary weight or bulk. I also consider sodium and how dinner fits into my entire day’s food plan, including breakfast, lunch, snacks, drinks, and dessert. If a meal falls short in one area, I can make up for it elsewhere in my menu. The goal isn’t to find a perfect dinner, but to pack food you’ll enjoy eating that provides the energy and nutrients you need to keep hiking strong.

item.title: France protests updates: Is it safe to travel to Paris right now? What visitors need to know about the riots
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
This is a breaking news story with information up to date as of 22nd October 2026. If there is one thing that the French know how to do, it is fight for their rights. It’s not for the goodness of politicians' hearts that university fees in France are still €178 for a bachelor's degree – compared with tuition fees of up to £9,790 a year in England for a standard course – but thanks to a population that refuses to back down when their rights are being threatened. Since September, French high-school students have been fighting for better conditions, especially in suburban areas often forgotten by institutions. The movement has reached almost unprecedented proportions, with other sectors joining the students, demanding better learning conditions, fighting against the cost-of-living crisis, the hike in fuel prices and the erosion of social welfare. The unrest has continued into the week, prompting the French government to introduce further security measures. On Monday 19 October, the Préfecture de Police imposed an overnight curfew in parts of central Paris, including areas around Place de la République and Les Halles, from 11pm until 6am the following morning and ban on demonstrations in certain areas of the capital. Since then, the restrictions have since been extended. Today, 22 October, the Préfecture de Police also banned unauthorised demonstrations and gatherings between 8am and 8pm in several parts of central Paris, including areas around the Louvre, Champs-Élysées, Élysée Palace, Bastille, République and major railway stations. The restrictions apply to demonstrations and gatherings rather than tourists visiting these areas. Meanwhile, high school students have called for further days of action on 22 and 24 October, as well as 3 and 5 November, raising the possibility of further disruption in the coming weeks. The government is also stepping up its response to the violence. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held talks with trade union representatives on Wednesday 21 October, although the discussions ended without an announced breakthrough. Financial assistance is being prepared for businesses affected by the unrest, alongside funding to repair damaged public facilities. An inquiry has also been launched into the handling of the demonstrations and the police response, as questions continue to be raised about the security arrangements during Saturday's protests. Following the weekend's violence, localised curfews have also been introduced in several other French cities, including Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille and Nice. In Lyon, restrictions covering part of the central Presqu'île district, from the Hôtel de Ville to Place Carnot, were imposed between 9pm and 6am on Monday night and subsequently renewed for Wednesday night. Similar measures have been introduced in other parts of France, with some curfews applying to everyone within designated areas and others targeting unaccompanied minors. On Thursday 22 October, several Metro stations were closed from 10am at the request of the Préfecture de Police, including Bastille, Saint-Paul, Place d'Italie, Campo Formio, Saint-Marcel, Quai de la Rapée, Gare d'Austerlitz, Bréguet-Sabin and Chemin Vert. Services on Metro Line 10 were also interrupted between Gare d'Austerlitz and Jussieu. These closures follow restrictions earlier in the week at major transport interchanges, including République and Châtelet–Les Halles, where trains were unable to stop. Travellers should check the latest RATP updates before setting off, as further closures may be introduced at short notice. With further demonstrations planned for Saturday 24 October, the French government is preparing a substantial security operation, including armoured vehicles, specialist police and gendarmerie units, and military personnel from Operation Sentinelle. Further restrictions on demonstrations are also expected in some cities. I have seen many protests during my years in France, but nothing like what’s unfolding right now. It’s important, however, to distinguish between peaceful demonstrators and those involved in vandalism, violence or looting. Although not always of this magnitude, violence and looting have also marred some previous large-scale gatherings in France, whether it’s France winning a football match or students fighting for their rights. What is happening in other parts of France? Paris is far from the only French city to have been affected by the recent unrest. On Saturday 17 October, demonstrations took place across the country, with an estimated 550,000 people taking to the streets according to the French authorities, although organisers put the figure at 800,000. While many of the marches remained peaceful, violence, vandalism and looting broke out in several major cities, including Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille. In Lyon, more than 20,000 people gathered for demonstrations that descended into violent clashes with police. One of the most shocking incidents took place at Place Bellecour, where a branch of the city's tourist office was vandalised and set on fire after a group of people forced their way inside. Dozens of shops across the Presqu'île, Lyon's central peninsula, were also damaged and looted. In Limoges, in south-western France, the historic Hôtel de Ville was devastated by a fire during the unrest. The 19th-century building, parts of which are protected as historic monuments, suffered extensive damage to its roof structure and central gable, with local authorities warning that it had not yet been saved. Elsewhere, protesters forced their way into Marseille's town hall, damaging the interior, while similar incidents were reported at municipal buildings in Lille and Angers. Shops were also targeted in several other cities. The violence has raised concerns within France's tourism industry, particularly as the country enters the Toussaint school holidays. According to Le Monde, some hotels have already reported cancellations and early departures, although the overall impact on bookings remains limited for now. Should you still travel to Paris? Does that mean Paris – and France as a whole – is now a no-go zone? No, it doesn’t. Certain streets and neighbourhoods may be affected by demonstrations, police operations or temporary closures, but the disruption is not necessarily city-wide. You can still come to Paris during this time and enjoy yourself, provided you keep informed and keep your wits about you when navigating the city. You might have to change some of your plans, but the good thing about Paris is that you can be here for decades, like me, and still discover new beautiful corners. France protests: Here is what to do if you are travelling to Paris When visiting a city, we all tend to want to stay as central as possible, but this is not a good idea when protests are happening. "Travellers should also think beyond their immediate surroundings: if a primary transportation route becomes inaccessible, do they know how to reach their accommodations or contact someone for assistance? Maintaining situational awareness and having a contingency plan can make a meaningful difference when circumstances change unexpectedly," says John Gobbels, CEO of air medical transport & security response membership program, Medjet. Avoid booking a hotel close to main squares or places of particular significance such as République, Bastille, Nation and Place de Clichy. Paris is not big and quite easy to navigate from wherever you are – at this time, choose to stay in quieter, residential areas. I suggest residential areas on the Rive Gauche like the 15th and 14th, or the 13th arrondissements. I particularly like the 15th as it has a lot of cute boutique hotels, and it’s close to some lovely places to visit like the Musée Bourdelle. Although authorised peaceful demonstrations are planned in advance, looters do not give a heads up before they take to the streets, so make sure you keep an eye on French news. "Once in the country, travellers should check local news, government, travel advisories and transport updates before heading out, particularly when demonstrations are expected near major attractions or transport hubs. Keep your phone charged, save emergency contacts offline, and be prepared to adjust your itinerary as conditions warrant. If you encounter a demonstration, avoid the crowd, move away calmly and follow local authorities’ instruction," suggests Gobbels. For metro closures and issues with public transport, check the Bonjour RATP website, while the Préfecture de Police also publishes information about demonstrations, traffic restrictions and security measures – it’s worth following them on X for immediate information. When it comes to news outlets, Franceinfo and Le Monde are reliable French news outlets, so it’s good to keep an eye on their websites. Although outlets such as Le Monde publish in English, their French-language coverage may offer more frequent local updates. I know it’s sad not to be able to stick to your plans, but for your safety it is better to avoid certain areas and attractions while protests are unfolding. Big institutions like the Louvre – which was blocked by students on Monday 19 October – and the Élysée Palace are better avoided; instead, visit some of the city's niche sights and smaller museums. Instead of the Louvre or the Musée d’Orsay, you could visit the beautiful Musée Gustave Moreau in the 9th or the Musée Zadkine in the 6th, depending on where you are staying. Big touristy spots like the Eiffel Tower are open and busy – if you don’t feel comfortable but still want a picture with the Eiffel Tower in the background, head to Île aux Cygnes to see the tiny Statue of Liberty and the Tower in all her glory, but from a safe distance.

item.title: Forget the front desk: Hilton Honors launches in-app points redemptions for digital checkout
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Hilton is making it easier than ever to use your points to pay for charges on your stay, and you don't even have to go to the front desk to do it. Hilton has launched the new "Pay with Points" program, offering Hilton Honors members the chance to use points to pay for part their bill while using digital checkout in the Hilton Honors App. But there's a caveat: Pay with Points is only available to elite members with Hilton Honors Silver, Gold, Diamond or Diamond Reserve status. Pay with Points is initially rolling out to 150 properties participating in the program across the United States. At this time, Hilton was unable to share a list of those properties but a Hilton Honors spokesperson said that properties in all categories of the Hilton portfolio, including luxury, lifestyle and resort properties are participating, and that "eligible Hilton Honors members will be notified via prearrival email if the hotel is participating in the Pay with Points test." The program is expected to expand to 800 properties by the end of the year and over 6,000 in 2027 throughout the U.S. and Canada. If folks are eligible to use Pay with Points, any eligible charges on the bill, including food, drinks, spa and more, can be paid for digitally with points. Now the question is: Is this a good use of Hilton Honors points? At the moment, Hilton is not sharing a specific points-to-dollar conversion rate, though the Hilton spokesperson told TPG that the program "gives Hilton Honors members more flexibility to use their Points in the way that works best for them." Hilton, it seems, is the first major loyalty program to offer the chance to use points digitally to pay for incidental charges, but Marriott Bonvoy and World of Hyatt members have ways to do it as well — and with a fixed rate. World of Hyatt members can "redeem points for a pre-determined dollar value award that can be used as a credit toward eligible redemption charges in participating Hyatt outlets," according to Hyatt's website. Hyatt has its own conversion chart where 1,000 World of Hyatt points converts into $10 to use towards the bill at physical checkout. If you need less than $75, each points is valued at 1 cent, with better redemption value at higher tiers (up to a maximum value of about 1.5 cents per point). It's not great and also not terrible; TPG values World of Hyatt points in October 2026 at 1.65 cents per point. Marriott Bonvoy members can do the same, using a fixed chart with pretty low per-point value: 250 Marriott Bonvoy points convert to $1, 2,500 points convert to $10, and 25,000 points convert to $100 for a fixed rate of 0.4 cents per point, which is well below TPG's October 2026 valuation for Marriott Bonvoy points at 0.75 cents apiece. Whether Hilton Honors Pay with Points is a good value or not remains to be seen, but what is good is seeing the program give members more choice for how they pay and a convenient way to do so. "Our Hilton Honors members have told us they want more flexibility when it comes to using those points," Brad Anderson, vice president of Hilton Honors, said in a statement. "They can already redeem them for free night stays or money-can’t-buy experiences around the world. Pay with Points introduces another digitally-enabled tool to our members, reducing the friction of travel and providing them with the choice and control that they value." Elite Hilton Honors members can now pay for incidental charges at select hotels using points and the Hilton Honors app. While the value of those points is unclear, as is the current list of properties where this option is available, Hilton deserves credit for giving members more flexibility for points redemptions.
