item.title: A beginners guide to visiting Skagway by cruise ship
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Skagway is a tiny town with a larger-than-life history. Nestled at the northern end of Lynn Canal, a 2,000-foot-deep fjord that extends for 90 miles through Alaska’s Inside Passage, Skagway was thrust onto the world stage during the frantic Klondike Gold Rush of 1898. Tens of thousands of stampeders arrived here from Seattle and beyond using what was then a remote outpost as the jumping-off point for the arduous journey into Canada’s Yukon. Almost overnight, Skagway transformed from a patch of forest into a rough-and-ready boomtown of saloons, gaming parlors and brothels, with a population topping 20,000. The frenzy was short lived. By the summer of 1899, the boom had ended, and most fortune seekers moved on to Nome and other areas or returned home, leaving behind a town of just 700 residents. More than a century later, Skagway still only has about 1,100 current residents. But its popularity as an Alaska cruise port has never been greater. The compact historic center is lined with brightly painted heritage buildings that house galleries, souvenir shops, restaurants and bars — all within easy walking distance of the harborfront Today, Skagway blends colorful Gold Rush history with spectacular scenery and outdoor adventure. You can ride the legendary White Pass & Yukon Route Railway into the mountains, hike sections of the original stampeders trail or simply wander the lively downtown streets soaking up the town’s distinctive personality. Here's everything you need to know before visiting one of Alaska's most memorable cruise ports. - It has an authentic, old-fashioned gold rush vibe, thanks to downtown’s handsome historic buildings. - Visitors have the chance to go on an epic train ride on the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway. - There is easy access to wilderness in both Alaska and northwestern British Columbia and the Yukon in Canada. - The tiny downtown can feel quite crowded when multiple ships dock at once. - Even in summer, the weather in Skagway can change quickly, and chilly winds and rain clouds sometimes funnel through Lynn Canal. - Language: English. - Currency: U.S. dollar. Credit cards are widely accepted. - Weather and packing: Expect daytime highs in the 60s during peak cruise season (June to August), with cooler mornings and evenings. Rain showers are common even on sunny days. It’s a good idea to pack layers and a waterproof jacket and to wear comfortable closed-toe walking shoes. - Time zone: Skagway is on Alaska Standard Time, which is an hour behind U.S. Pacific Standard Time, and it observes daylight saving time. Up to four cruise ships can dock simultaneously at Skagway's port along Lynn Canal. The port has several berths, all within walking distance of downtown. Broadway Dock and Ore Dock are the closest, just a five- to 10-minute walk. Railroad Dock is the furthest and the one most often used by megaships. From here, it’s about a 10- to 15-minute walk into town, though complimentary cruise line shuttles are often available. Skagway’s low-cost SMART shuttle also runs between Railroad Dock and downtown for around $3 one-way. Many shore excursions depart directly from the piers. If you’re taking an excursion that crosses into Canada (the border is just 15 miles north of town), be sure to bring your passport with you. You can get a good sense of Skagway’s easygoing personality and engaging gold rush history in an hour or two by walking from the cruise docks into downtown. Most passengers combine a stroll through this atmospheric community with a meal at a convivial restaurant and a ride on the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway (or some other outdoorsy adventure). As you walk into town from your ship, the Skagway Centennial Statue at the corner of Broadway and First Avenue in Centennial Park is a good place to start. Across the street, stop by the beautifully restored White Pass & Yukon Railway Depot, an 1898 building that now serves as the Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park museum. The museum's photos, films, memorabilia and well-crafted exhibits tell the story of the wild stampede for gold that led to the town’s founding. As you make your way north up Broadway, you can admire many of the town’s most striking historic buildings, some of which date all the way back to the 1898 gold rush. These include the rollicking Red Onion Saloon and the gilt-dome Golden North Hotel (inside which you’ll find Corrington’s Museum of Alaskan History, with its impressive collection of carved-ivory scrimshaw). The Arctic Brotherhood Hall, one of the most eye-catching structures you’ll pass, was built in 1900 using nearly 9,000 pieces of driftwood. Inside, you’ll find a visitor center run by the town’s tourism office. Nearby, the stately Skagway Museum contains exhibits that provide an overview of the town’s history beyond just the gold rush era, from Native American artifacts to artwork from more recent times. Inside the historic Eagles Hall, you can attend a performance of "The Days of '98 with Soapy Smith," an over-the-top history burlesque of sorts (complete with a can-can dance revue) that’s been performed here since 1923. You can also take a peek inside the Moore Cabin, the town’s oldest building (dating to 1887), which is administered by the National Park Service. If you're looking to stretch your legs a bit more, walk or take the city bus to Gold Rush Cemetery, at the north end of downtown, where you can see the gravesites of Soapy Smith, Frank Reid and other pioneers. From here, it’s just a few minutes’ stroll beneath a dense canopy of trees to view the refreshing cascades at Lower Reid Falls. If you’ve booked a ride on the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway, head to the station at Broadway and Second Avenue, where trains depart. This narrow-gauge railway climbs almost 3,000 feet in just 20 miles, offering views of waterfalls, glaciers and trestle bridges. Visitors who have an extra hour or two can make the short side trip to Dyea (pronounced dye-EE), about 7 miles west of downtown. There, you can hike a bit of the Chilkoot Trail, a legendary 33-mile route that prospectors once used to make their way into Canada’s Yukon. Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park administers Dyea and offers tours of this noteworthy historic site. By far, the most popular shore excursions involve a ride on the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway. However, there are many other rugged, outdoorsy adventures, such as zip-lining and hiking, as well as easygoing history tours. Train ride on the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway A variety of excursions include a scenic ride aboard one of the restored or replica vintage rail cars that have been plying these narrow-gauge tracks since 1898. The most popular option is a roughly three-hour narrated round-trip excursion through the verdant landscape up to the 2,865-foot White Pass Summit, at the U.S.-Canada border. Longer options, lasting up to a full day, continue farther into British Columbia and the Yukon and generally cost $200 to $300 or more per adult. Many combine the train ride with add-ons such as bus tours, ghost town visits, gold-panning at a historic prospector's camp, visits to First Nations communities, salmon bakes and barbecues or a bike ride along a stretch of the Klondike Highway. Although not as famous as Juneau for this activity, Skagway has become an increasingly popular port for glacier touring. These trips last about two hours and include a helicopter ride over the northern end of the enormous Juneau Icefield for a bird’s-eye view over Chilkat, Ferebee, Meade and other dramatic glaciers before landing on a glacier for a short walk. You can also book a more deluxe version of this trip, the highlight of which is a dogsledding experience on Denver Glacier, during which you'll interact with the dogs and their puppies, meet with competitive Iditarod racers, and watch a mushing demonstration across the ice. Prices start at about $439 per person for a glacier landing and walk, while helicopter tours that include a visit to a dogsledding camp on Denver Glacier generally start around $599 per person and can exceed $800 per person when booked through a cruise line. Visit a musher's camp in historic Dyea to learn about dogsledding, which has a long and venerable tradition in Alaska. This is a dry-land experience (there's no snow), and typically costs $165 to $210 per person. Huskies lead you down an exhilarating mile-long trail through Tongass National Forest. Some tours offer the addition of a gold-panning experience. This is a great choice for adrenaline seekers. Tour options include a 20-minute van ride north of town to a rainforest adventure park with a ropes course and six zip lines that whizz you through the surrounding treetops. Fares range from about $160 to $215 per person. Another option takes you on a half-day trip to Dyea for $260 per adult. Ride an all-wheel-drive Unimog up a rugged mountain road through a lush rainforest to Grizzly Falls. From here, you’ll make your way back down the mountainside via a course of 10 zip lines and four suspension bridges. Hike along the Chilkoot Trail with a river float On this moderately strenuous half-day adventure costing $180 to $200 per person, you'll hike a dramatic stretch of historic Chilkoot Trail used by stampeders during the 1898 Klondike Gold Rush. Then, you'll hop into an inflatable raft for a leisurely, picturesque float journey down the Taiya River to the estuary at Dyea. Note: There are no rapids or white water on this section of the river. Best Skagway outdoor activities near the cruise port It’s easy to get out and explore nature on your own within a short distance of the cruise docks. There are a few popular rambles that take just an hour or two to complete and are great for families and hikers seeking a mellow outing. Walking to Yakutania Point and Smuggler's Cove This easy 1 1/2-mile, out-and-back trek along a level trail begins downtown at the south end of Skagway’s small airport. It crosses a scenic pedestrian bridge and then bends around a rocky, wooded peninsula with dramatic vistas of Lynn Canal. The simplest version of this experience involves hiking about half a mile from downtown to the edge of narrow Lower Dewey Lake, which is flanked by rising forested hills on each side. If you want to experience even more awesome panoramas, make a complete circumnavigation of this serene lake. The full loop from downtown is about 3 1/2 miles, and the trail switches back steeply at one point, with an overall elevation gain of around 800 feet. Sockeye Cycle, which is right in downtown Skagway, rents e-bikes and a wide variety of road and mountain bikes. You can use them to explore the area, whether right in town, out to Dyea or up the Klondike Highway to White Pass. It also offers a range of cycling tours. Klondike Electric Bicycles is another e-bike rental option. For a glacier experience that you can manage at your own pace, book a ride on the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway; hop out at Glacier Station (mile 14), and then hike for several miles on a moderately challenging eight-mile, out-and-back trail to Laughton Glacier. This is a full-day adventure, so it's only feasible if your ship is in port for at least nine hours. You could also do a quicker (though more expensive) hike to Laughton by booking a flightseeing helicopter ride to Glacier Station with Packer Expeditions and then returning by train. - On foot: Downtown Skagway is compact, and it's an easy five- to 10-minute walk from the cruise docks. - Bus: There are no taxis or ride-hailing services in this tiny town, but Skagway Municipal and Regional Transit buses run between the cruise docks and downtown all day while ships are in port; the fare is $3 one-way or $5 for an all-day ticket. Additionally, the Skagway Street Car Company offers narrated 90-minute tours of the town’s historic sites and attractions on restored bright-yellow 1920s buses. - Car: There are a few car rental agencies in town, but daily rates are steep ($250 and up during the cruise ship season), and inventory is limited. For a day visit, a car isn’t really necessary unless you want to embark on your own road trip up the Klondike Highway into Canada. Carcross, Yukon, is the nearest town of interest (about 90 minutes from Skagway); it’s another hour to Yukon’s capital, Whitehorse. Cruise ships generally visit Skagway for around eight to 12 hours, so a longer drive is doable, but try to book a few weeks before the day your cruise will be in port to ensure availability. Skagway restaurants near the cruise port For a small town, Skagway punches well above its weight when it comes to dining. Expect consistently good food and a convivial old-school atmosphere in the town’s restaurants. In addition to pouring first-rate IPAs, Belgian dark ales and heady barley wines, the warmly lit Skagway Brewing Company prepares some of the tastiest gastropub fare in town; consider the pork belly kimchi burger or macaroni and cheese with rock crab. A rowdy gold rush-era brothel that’s now a full-service tavern, the Red Onion Saloon is justly celebrated for its 16-inch pizzas, cold beer and saucy atmosphere. For creative farm-to-table cooking in a dapper dining room, book a table at Olivia’s Bistro, inside the Historic Skagway Inn. For more casual bites, head to Peppers Street Fusion for hefty California-style burritos and street tacos with intriguing fillings like chimichurri halibut and chorizo with corn salsa. At 1898 Burgers N' Shakes, you can get mammoth smash burgers topped with smoked salmon and green chiles, as well as milkshakes in offbeat flavors like rhubarb and spruce tip. Overlooking the town’s picturesque small boat harbor, The Skagway Fish Company and the Salty Siren are top choices for succulent local shellfish and finfish. This is yet another Inside Passage port that’s ideal for sampling wild Alaskan seafood, from halibut chowder to smoked salmon pate to King crab bisque. Alaskan fry bread, which is served hot and dusted with cinnamon sugar, is a Skagway specialty. Folks line up for it at the funky Klondike Doughboy bakery, which is also a fine place to pick up local jams, honeys, birch syrup and taffy. To sample another specialty of the Last Frontier, stop by the adorable Skagway Weenie Wagon food truck for a reindeer sausage hot dog topped with grilled onions. And for a sip of pure Alaskan goodness, order a Spruce Tip Blonde Ale — savoring its citrusy and piney notes — at the Skagway Brewing Company. Steps from the cruise docks, Broadway is lined with boutiques and galleries for about six blocks, starting at Centennial Park. You’ll find old-fashioned mercantiles, jewelry shops, trading posts and crafts galleries along this stretch; Indigenous-owned Wild Yukon Furs and BearHead Photography Gallery are among the most popular and reputable spots. Popular keepsakes and wares include carvings, art and beadwork by Native Alaskan and First Nations artists, and jewelry that incorporates locally mined gold nuggets as well as ivory scrimshaw and jade. Free things to do in Skagway cruise port One of the most enjoyable ways to experience Skagway without spending anything is to stroll through the historic downtown, admiring the colorfully painted gold rush-era buildings and visiting the free Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park. Other free-admission spots are downtown’s Pullen Creek StreamWalk (where you can spy salmon valiantly fighting their way upstream during their late-summer runs), Yakutania Point via the Skagway River Footbridge and the historic Gold Rush Cemetery. Does the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway sell out? Yes, especially the White Pass Summit Excursion, which often sells out during peak summer sailings. Book ahead through your cruise line's shore excursion desk or directly with the railway rather than waiting to buy tickets in port. Do I need my passport for excursions that stay in the U.S.? No. You won't need a passport for excursions that remain in Alaska, such as the standard White Pass Summit round-trip, musher camp visits, zip-lining adventures or Chilkoot Trail hike-and-float tours. However, bring your passport if your excursion crosses into British Columbia or the Yukon, including Fraser and Carcross rail extensions and drives along the Klondike Highway. How much port time do I need for the full Yukon rail excursion? Longer train excursions that continue into Fraser or Carcross can take most of the day. Since Skagway port calls typically last eight to 12 hours, these trips are usually feasible, but check your ship's arrival and all-aboard times before booking to ensure you have a comfortable buffer. Do I need to hire a car to see Skagway in a day? No. Downtown Skagway is within easy walking distance of the cruise pier, and most major attractions and shore excursions include transportation to and from the port. Tiny though it is, Skagway delivers an outsize Alaska experience and a fascinating glimpse into its gold rush days. Breathtaking mountain scenery that you can soak up from an iconic vintage railway journey is another great reason to choose a cruise itinerary that calls on this welcoming little town.

item.title: Palatial but personalized in Perth: A review of Como The Treasury
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Palatial but personalized in Perth: A review of Como The Treasury It may be smack dab in the center of Perth, but Como The Treasury feels more like a spa retreat than your average city hotel. Part of its idiosyncrasy is because, rather than occupying a modern tower, it is located in the sprawling State Buildings, which were constructed between 1875-1959 and housed, as you may have guessed from the name, the former State Treasury of Western Australia, the Land Titles office and the Post Office, among other official outposts. But this luxurious redoubt, which opened in 2015, has zen-like interiors courtesy of Australian design firm Kerry Hill Architects, an impressive collection of contemporary Australian art and an oasis-like spa that will soothe away the aches and pains of the long journey required to get to Perth (from pretty much anywhere). It's well worth going that distance, though, to luxuriate in the expansive guest accommodations and to enjoy an unhurried dinner composed of intriguing Australian ingredients at its signature restaurant, Wildflower. That's just the beginning of what's in store during a stay at Como The Treasury Perth, though. Here's what else you can expect. - The vibe: Colonial-era grandeur on the outside, well-curated contemporary art gallery on the inside mixed with the lively energy of the downtown work crowd drifting through the public areas to grab coffee and lunch during the day and cocktails and leisurely dinners by night. - The location: The hotel is located in the middle of the city's central business district (CBD), across a square from the cathedral and the City of Perth Library, and within walking distance to Elizabeth Quay for ferries to Rottnest Island and major museums in the city's cultural precinct. - Getting there: The hotel is approximately a 30-minute drive from Perth Airport (PER). Taxis and Ubers cost around 40-50 Australian dollars ($28-$35) each way. - Parking: Limited valet parking is available for AU$80 ($56) per night. - Size: There hotel has just 48 rooms and suites, including just two starter-level City rooms, while the rest are larger Heritage and Treasury rooms and suites, including some with features like balconies overlooking Cathedral Square. - Food and drink: The two main restaurants associated with the hotel are the fine-dining Wildflower and more casual bistro Post (where breakfast is served), but guests can enjoy a handful of other restaurants attached to the property that are part of the State Buildings Precinct. - Pet policy: Only service animals are allowed. Como The Treasury Perth has a mere 48 rooms. There are two in the smallest City category, which still measure up at a respectable 500 square feet. The rest are divided into Heritage and Treasury rooms, depending on their view and location, with categories including those with balconies as well as larger residential-style suites including two-bedroom Family Suites. My Treasury Balcony room was located on the eastern facade of the building overlooking St. George's Cathedral and the architecturally interesting City of Perth Library. It was a palatial 700 square feet including a huge bedroom with a breakfast table, a separate workdesk, a well-stocked minibar and French doors that opened up onto the private balcony. The king-size bed was made up with crisp Egyptian cotton linens, and the overall palette of silver, taupe and cream lent the whole space a spa-like feel. As did the enormous bathroom, which was tiled in travertine with a dramatic, oversize walk-in shower and an elliptical freestanding bathtub, all provisioned with Como's own Shambhala bath and body products. The vast space felt like a cozy private sanctum in the center of the city, and once the blackout curtains were closed and the windows latched, it became the perfect respite for an undisturbed night's sleep. Como The Treasury Perth is a dining destination unto itself thanks not only to the extraordinary menus of native Australian ingredients at Wildflower, but also because it is attached to the State Buildings Precinct, a vibrant public space with several restaurants, bars and cafes as well as a lovely little gift shop. Located on the hotel's fourth-floor rooftop with beautiful views down to Elizabeth Quay and the Swan River and stunning murals depicting Western Australian flora by artist Valerie Sparks, Wildflower is one of the most unique restaurants in the city. The menu changes six times a year in accordance with the traditional Indigenous seasons and many dishes feature native Australian ingredients. During my stay in August, we were in the midst of Djilba, which is a little like springtime, when plants start blooming and migratory birds begin to nest. In addition to a diverse list of unique Australian wines from around the continent, we were treated to a multicourse tasting menu of dishes like luscious scallops from Esperance with shiitake mushrooms and finger limes; earthy sunchokes accompanied by desert lime, smoked egg yolk and grassy chive oil; line-caught snapper with artichoke, lemon myrtle and mellow vin jaune; and juicy lamb with herbaceous warrigal, asparagus and courgettes. Dessert consisted of an 80% dark chocolate mousse with macadamia crumble, crunch black barley and banana. It was one of the most memorable dinners I've had in Australia over the course of nearly two decades of visits. Located adjacent to the hotel in the State Buildings, Post is a casual all-day bistro where hotel guests can enjoy sumptuous breakfasts as well as hearty but elegant lunch and dinner menus of Italian classics. Breakfast included plates of fresh fruit and pastry baskets then a choice of made-to-order dishes such as avocado toast (this is Australia, after all) on seed and nut bread and warming steel-cut porridge with cinnamon, almonds, honey and fruit compote, as well as a selection of coffee drinks, teas and fresh-pressed juices. The hotel has a series of small private rooms that feel like a cross between a study and a parlor where guests can partake of the "Artful Afternoon Tea" inspired by the colorful ink and watercolor paintings that adorn the walls by Australian artists Alex and Philippa Nikulinsky. Attached to the hotel, the State Buildings are a large public hub with several bars and restaurants that Como guests can also enjoy. The venues include Long Chim for contemporary Thai in a buzzy setting, beer corner for brews and pub grub, the wine merchant for glasses of vino and small plates and Petition, which is more of an upscale brasserie where we dined on specialties like terrine of salmon and Shark Bay prawns with dill cream, cucumber and brioche; and lightly fried chicken with carrot and ginger puree and a side of Brussels sprouts. Como the Treasury Perth has several other fabulous amenities worth noting. - First and foremost is an outpost of Como's Shambhala Spa, which is located near the lobby in the former 19th-century vaults. There, guests can indulge in treatments utilizing Como's own products as well as Australian lines like Sodashi and Rationale. - There is a well-equipped gym and a long lap pool with moody city views through two-story floor-to-ceiling windows. - The reception area is like a little art gallery and living room combined, where guests are greeted with a glass of Champagne at check-in and invited to lounge anytime they like. - The gift shop carries adorable sundries from Australian craftspeople that make for excellent souvenirs. - Service is professional, polished and polite, but with that genuine Australian warmth you'd expect. Nightly rates at Como The Treasury Perth start at AU$747 ($520) per night for a City room, while the Treasury Balcony room I was in starts at AU$1,377 ($955). Como The Treasury Perth is part of American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, so if you have American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express, you can make a booking through amextravel.com and receive perks like availability-based upgrades, up to a $100 credit to use on-property during your stay for things like drinks or meals, complimentary daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout. Both cards now offer a semiannual $300 (up to $600 per calendar year) statement credit on prepaid stays at Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts, so you could save $300 on a reservation at this hotel if you are able to take advantage of one of these cards' credits. The hotel is also a member of Capital One's Premier Collection. So if you have the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card or the Capital One Venture X Business, you can book a stay through Capital One Travel for value-added benefits like free daily breakfast for two, up to $100 in on-property experience credits and room upgrades (if available). Although it is located in a historic building, Como The Treasury Perth has ramps and elevators so that guests with mobility requirements can access all the guestroom floors and hotel amenities. There are rooms available with mobility, vision and hearing accessibility features. As always, though, it is best to contact the hotel directly to ensure that any accommodations or other spaces meet your specific requirements. Although Perth has other luxury hotels including a soaring Ritz-Carlton and the blingy Crown Tower, Como The Treasury Perth provides the city's most distinctive stay. The heritage buildings in which it housed create a truly unique setting, while the calm, capacious rooms, welcoming spa and an entire precinct of hopping bars and restaurants all create a truly inviting, engaging ambience for a special stay in the Western Australian capital. item.title: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points Transferable rewards currencies, such as American Express Membership Rewards points, Chase Ultimate Rewards points, Citi ThankYou Rewards points and Bilt Points, consistently rank as some of the most valuable rewards in our monthly valuations. What makes these rewards particularly valuable is their ability to be transferred to various airline and hotel programs. If you look at our valuations, you'll notice that transferable rewards are generally worth more than the airline miles and hotel points you can transfer them to. For example, you can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at a 1:1 ratio. But because our October 2026 valuations value Chase points at 2.05 cents each and Virgin points at 1.5 cents each, you might think you're losing 0.55 cents per point with this transfer. However, that doesn't mean you're actually losing value when you transfer points. These valuations are estimates, and the value you'll get from a specific redemption could be much higher or lower. So, here's why transferable points are worth more than other types of rewards. Protect against individual program devaluations With so many devaluations, it's no secret that points and miles are a poor long-term investment. That's why we don't recommend hoarding points and miles. But if you want to build a stash of rewards for an upcoming trip, one of the best ways to protect yourself against devaluations is by earning transferable rewards. If you have a large balance of points or miles in a single loyalty program, a significant devaluation could substantially reduce the value of your rewards. But transferable rewards can help protect you against devaluations in individual airline and hotel loyalty programs. If one transfer partner increases its award rates, you may still get good value by transferring your rewards to another program. And because some airline and hotel programs partner with multiple transferable rewards currencies, you may have several ways to earn the points or miles you need for a particular redemption. Of course, transferable rewards aren't immune to devaluations, either, as issuers can change transfer partners, transfer ratios and redemption options. It's generally best to keep your rewards in a transferable currency until you've found an award you want to book. Most transfers to airline and hotel programs are irreversible, so you'll lose flexibility once you move your points or miles. Before transferring, confirm that the award you want is available and that you're happy with the redemption value. Flexibility to choose the best redemption Transferable rewards also give you more flexibility than any single airline or hotel loyalty program. For example, if you've been earning Delta SkyMiles on the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card, you'll need to redeem those miles through the SkyMiles program. Although you can redeem Delta Air Lines miles for flights operated by some partner airlines, you're still limited to the award pricing and availability that Delta offers. On the other hand, if you've been earning Ultimate Rewards points with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), you could transfer your points to various programs — including Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club — or redeem them through the Chase Travel℠ portal to book a paid flight. Likewise, if you earn American Express Membership Rewards points with a card like the American Express® Gold Card, you can transfer your points to multiple airline and hotel loyalty programs instead of being limited to a single program. Some transferable rewards programs also let you redeem points or miles for cash back, statement credits or other rewards, although these redemption options usually give you a lower redemption value. Transferable rewards currencies routinely offer transfer bonuses that let you transfer your rewards at a better ratio. For example, if a program normally transfers at a 1:1 ratio, a 20% transfer bonus would let you convert 10,000 transferable points or miles into 12,000 airline miles or hotel points. That means you'd need fewer transferable points to book the same award. Depending on what's available when you're ready to book, a favorable transfer bonus may boost the value you can get from your transferable rewards. However, it's still important to compare award prices and availability before transferring, as a transfer bonus doesn't necessarily make a redemption worthwhile. Transferable rewards are valuable because they give you options. Instead of being locked into a single airline or hotel loyalty program, you can compare award prices across multiple programs, take advantage of transfer bonuses and choose how to redeem your rewards when you're ready to book. Although transferable rewards aren't immune to devaluations, their flexibility makes them some of the most valuable rewards you can earn.

item.title: Winter Hiking Layering Guide
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
Wearing multiple clothing layers for winter or cold-weather hiking keeps you drier and warmer by moving moisture away from your skin. Sounds simple, right? It is, but many people struggle to understand the science behind layering and how it can guide your base-layer, mid-layer, and shell choices for winter hiking. Check out our clothing recommendations below. The core principle of layering is to dress like an onion, with multiple layers that manage moisture, retain heat, and protect you from the elements. - Baselayer garments sit directly against your skin and are designed to keep you dry by moving perspiration to the next layer, your mid-layer. - Mid-layer garments keep you warm, even though they absorb moisture from your baselayers. Some mid-layer garments are more breathable than others and can dry while you wear them, while others are designed purely for warmth and aren’t very breathable. We discuss this further below. - Finally, an outer shell layer protects against wind, rain, or snow. Baselayer clothing moves perspiration away from your skin to prevent evaporative cooling. When moisture sits on your skin, it sucks heat out of your body as it tries to evaporate. That’s why perspiration makes you feel cooler in summer. You want to avoid that in winter. In winter, you want to move that moisture off your skin and through your base layer so your skin doesn’t touch wet fabric. That’s where a mid-layer comes in. The best mid-layers absorb moisture as it leaves your base layer. This is a process called wicking. Ideally, you want a mid-layer that stays warm when it absorbs moisture, or multiple mid-layer garments that do the same. Wicking works through capillary action, where a liquid is pulled from one layer to another without gravity’s influence. If you’ve ever dipped the corner of a sponge into a pool of water, the water is drawn into the sponge through this process. The strength of wicking between a base layer and a mid-layer depends on the mid-layer’s structure and absorbency. A porous mid-layer, like a fleece pullover, is very effective at pulling moisture out of a base layer garment because its many small pores suck in moisture like a sponge. The outermost layer, a shell, is usually the least wicking layer and is designed more for wind, rain, or snow protection. It may passively trap some of the warm air that escapes the mid-layer, but it’s usually not insulated. Here’s what the science of layering tells us about choosing winter hiking clothes. The best base layers absorb little perspiration and wick it efficiently to your mid-layer. Synthetic jerseys and long underwear are clear winners. Thinner baselayers are better than thicker ones because moisture has less distance to travel to your mid-layer. The same goes for more fitted baselayers than looser ones. If you can hold up a base layer jersey and see light coming through, that’s good. It’s even better if you can see the outlines of objects or furniture in the same room. Synthetic base layers hold up well over time: they’re inexpensive and easy to launder in a washing machine. My gotos are: Wool base layers hold onto moisture and take much longer to dry, even though they can feel warmer when they’re damp. As far as layering goes, a baselayer’s primary goal isn’t to keep you warm, but to move perspiration off your skin to the next layer. I know people like wool baselayers because they don’t smell as much, but on winter day hikes when icicles hang off my nose hair and beard, I’m more interested in wicking performance than body odor. Wool baselayers have other issues too, like high care and maintenance requirements (special soap, hand wash, hang dry), and they need replacing much more often than synthetic base layers. They are also a lot more expensive. I’m lucky if I can get two years out of a wool jersey, while I can easily get ten years or more out of synthetic ones. That’s a lot less trash in the landfill with none of the associated overhead of animal husbandry. Wool baselayers made with a combination of wool and synthetic yarns are a better choice than straight wool and there is a whole segment of the outdoor industry working to make wool suck less. Good examples include Smartwool Intraknit and the Nuyarn garments made by KUIU. Fleece mid-layer pullovers and hoodies beat wool because they dry quickly when exposed to air. The problem with fleece is that the outdoor industry has created so many proprietary variants that it’s impossible to know how well a garment will perform without trying it in the field. Gone are the days when all fleece was classified as being 100 gsm, 200 gsm, or 300 gsm and you knew exactly what you were getting. (GSM stands for grams per square meter and describes the weight of the fabric used) If you want a classic 100 gsm fleece, or something close, which is usually plenty for active hiking or snowshoeing, the less expensive fleece pullovers or jackets from REI, Patagonia, and Lands End are a good bet. This type of fleece is dense enough to block light wind and can serve as an outer layer in mild conditions. Fleece vests also make a great mid-layer because they keep your core warm while letting your arms, which need less warmth, breathe. Ultralight fleece, in the form of Polartec Alpha Direct Tops and Octa Fleece Hoodies, is another excellent option, available in 60 gsm, 90 gsm, or 120 gsm fabric weights, with 90 gsm as the sweet spot for winter hiking. Neither variety is very wind-resistant, unlike classic fleece, so you usually need to wear them under a windbreaker, softshell jacket, or hard shell. They are much lighter than classic fleece and wick better, which is their main attraction, especially for warmer-weather hiking. You can also buy wind-resistant softshell hooded jackets that are lined with Polartec Alpha Direct or Octa fleece. I can recommend the Octa-lined Arc’teryx Proton SL Softshell Hoody and the Polartec Alpha-lined Mammut Eiger Norwand IN Flex Air Hooded Jacket. These active-use jackets work well down to about 20F, as long as you expect “dry” precipitation like snow. Wool mid-layers can also work, including hoodies, although they wick and dry somewhat slower than their synthetic counterparts. While they hang in my closet, they’re just too warm and heavy for me to wear often. Still, they may be a good option if you run cold. Many hikers think insulated synthetic and down jackets make good mid-layer garments. While they are good passive layers to throw on if you take a break and want to ward off a chill, they make remarkably bad active mid-layers because you’ll be too warm if you try to hike in them; you’ll sweat like a pig and soak your base layer and the jacket liner. You are much better off wearing cooler layers that keep your base layer and mid-layer insulation drier all day. Winter hiking and snowshoeing generate a lot of body heat, and you won’t be cold if you’re moving. But don’t take my word for it. Go try it. That’s how everyone learns what they prefer when it comes to layering winter hiking clothes. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides.

item.title: Namibia' Black Rhino Is One of Africa’s Most Exciting Conservation Stories
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Weâd been looking for nearly five hoursâscanning the dry grass for upturned pebbles and the horizon for a dark, lumbering shapeâwhen we spotted the rhino bull. Next to me, tracker Mensley Karutjaiva shook his head with a resigned chuckle. Weâd been up since daybreak, alongside three other members of the Save the Rhino Trust, looking for critically endangered black rhinos in Damaraland, a land of flat-topped mountains, rocky hills, and stark plains in the Kunene region of northwestern Namibia. While we scrambled about in the heat, the bull had been dozing in the shade of a milk bush. We watched as he stood up, as if posing for us, before lying back down to resume his nap. I was traveling in a loop around northwest Namibia that took me to three new (or recently renewed) camps. Since photographic safari tourism began here over a century ago, Namibia has largely been known amongst international travelers as a self-drive vacationâa destination with plenty of do-it-yourself road trips through otherworldly desert landscapes. Unknown to many visitors, though, human-wildlife conflictâpopulation activities that negatively affect animals through habitat loss or resource competitionâ has been an ongoing challenge, and past decades of poaching threw rhinoceros populations into a tailspin. But, in the past few years, Namibia has seen a lot of positive conservation momentum, with these northwest reaches acting as a bellwether. From innovative government measures to an Indigenous-stewarded private reserve, this region is now a story of forward-looking change. In May 2026, the countryâs government launched a new conservation finance deal called Namibia for Life in partnership with the World Wildlife Fund. Worth approximately $63 million, it sets aside funds for Namibiaâs 86 community-supported conservancies, which span more than 49 million acres. Gazing at the black rhino, I felt a thrill as my eyes followed the magnificent swoop of the animalâs two intact horns, the larger of the two over three feet long. In an attempt to deter poachers, wildlife management will often cut down a rhinosâ hornsâa humane, if humbling, procedureâso that the sight of a rhino, especially one of this critically endangered sub-species, often entails seeing just nubs. Rhino horn can fetch up to $5,400 a pound in the illegal wildlife tradeâso just seeing this intact horn was a triumph in itself. Decimated by poaching throughout the 1970s and 80s due to demand in Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, wild black rhino populations had dropped by 96 percent in the mid 90s. They came so close to extinction that only 2,410 were left on the entire planet. That sighting was a harbinger of better days to come. Thanks to conservation efforts, today some 6,000 black rhinos now roam free, with an estimated half of those living in Namibia. In July 2026, the World Wildlife Fund announced that Namibia had experienced a 53 percent drop in rhino poaching since 2024, reaching its lowest numbers of rhino poaching instances in over a decade. âOver the past 39 years of visiting Namibia regularly, Iâve been heartened to see a growing understanding of the importance of conservation and community-based tourismâand more recently, how to sustain it,â said travel advisor Nicola Shepherd, who arranged my itinerary. âNamibian organizations such as the nonprofit Integrated Rural Development and Nature Conservation are investing in practical ways to reduce conflict and protect both people and wildlife.â The founder of the conservation-focused Explorations Company, Shepherd and her team have been arranging customized trips to this country for decades. In the past few years, sheâs noted a shift in the advent of luxury accommodations, including Zannier Hotels, Habitas, and others, that have broadened the country's appeal to travelers seeking high-end experiences. Itâs all welcome news for the country, which is experiencing an uptick in traveler interestâjust two months after my trip, local publications reported that the countryâs hotel room occupancy was having one of its strongest years. More than twice the size of California, Namibiaâs expanse includes coastline, semi-arid desert, dry and wet woodlands, and golden savanna. The northwest corner is a rich mix of these terrainsâincluding the otherworldly, white-tipped grasslands I walked through as we returned to Wilderness Desert Rhino Camp after our morning rhino sighting. âIn this area of the Palmwag Concession, the rotation of tourism helps protect rhinos,â Karutjaiva told me. I heard this sentiment echoed wherever I went, although specific numbers are carefully guarded. âItâs a state secret. The only thing I can say is that the population is growing,â he said. The guardedness is understandable, as the threat of poaching is still everywhere. And growth isnât restricted to the rhino populations. At Desert Rhino Camp, a full rebuild in 2024 resulted in six stand-alone tented suites, where materials like timber, leather, and stone evoke a modern, desert-chic style. With the Etendeka Mountains rising in the distance, red basalt boulders form the walls of the open-air dining lounge where I enjoyed a delicious slow-cooked lamb potjie stew for dinner. âWe really realized how important tourism was during the pandemic, when most businesses closed and a lot of people lost their jobs,â lodge manager Fanus Katondoka told me that evening, as we sipped on rooibos iced teas. âNow we know it. Operators are building a lot of facilities, lodges, hotelsâit's booming.â That growth means more resources for community-supported conservation, so Karutjaiva and his team can continue their work protecting rhinos and other species. Rhinos have adorned conservation headlines recently, but theyâre far from the only draw in northwest Namibia. A new camp from outfitter Natural Selection recently opened about an hourâs flight north, in the desert Kaokoveld region, highlighting another species of desert-adapted wildlife. A few days later, I was headed to see it. Sitting in the cockpit seat of a tiny four-seater Cessna, I waved goodbye to the rhino trackers and flew over the Namib Desert, one of the oldest arid regions in the world. The landscape flowed in ridges and mountains of faded yellow and whisper pink, where welwitschiaâlarge, low-lying plants that live to be hundreds of years oldâsprawled like relics from a Dune film set. It was a fitting introduction to my next stop: the Hoanib Valley, home to a new camp with a mission thatâs a bit bigger than rhinoceros. I quickly learned what that something was when guide Howard Groenewaldt picked me up from the airstrip, nosed our vehicle toward camp, and then abruptly cut the engine. We had stopped at the Hoanib River, a seasonal waterway that runs west from the desert until it reaches the Skeleton Coast on the Atlantic Ocean. Now in the dry season, it turned into a sandy avenue lined with camelthorn and giant ana trees that age more than 100 years old. It was a nature-born runwayâand something was stirring around a bend. A giant, desert-adapted elephant slowly walked toward us. His long tusks were pale white; the bottoms of his feet splayed out wide under his skinny legs, the better to stabilize on sand. There was no sound except the breeze that was stirring the wizened, banana-shaped seed pods in the branches above my head, and the soft fwump of the elephantâs footsteps. I watched, transfixed, as he paused and delicately trailed the tip of his trunk on the ground This is exactly the kind of encounter the new Natural Selection Hoanib Elephant Camp was built around. Located off the northern bank of the river, its 10 solar-powered suites bring a new level of comfort to the valley. Between game drives, guests here lounge on the veranda overlooking the desert hoping to spy more elephants, or relax in their suites with a massage or nap. Each of the natural-hued suites include a private plunge pool, a deep king-size bed, and a writing desk. Dinner is a multi-course affair in the shared lounge; afterward, a bonfire crackles under the stars. During my stay some visitors curled up on the couches against the evening desert chill, sipping hot drinks spiked with Amarula, a South African liqueur, surrounded by flickering candles. While the resort is stylish and deeply comfortable, Natural Selectionâs approach to community partnership also reflects the shift in this region toward local collaboration. The evening I arrived at camp, I met Petty Daniels, who hails from the nearby Torra Conservancy and brings an acutely local perspective. Years ago, she began working in hospitality as a waitressâtoday, sheâs the manager of both this new camp and its giraffe-focused sister property, the Hoanib Valley Camp. Roughly 97 percent of staff are from surrounding community conservancies, creating a working model of local investment in supporting companies that protect their homeland. Within Danielsâ generation, change has been flourishing in the hearts and minds of locals. âBefore tourism, people drove wherever they wanted, shooting animals to provide food for their families,â she said. âNot anymore. People are getting into conservation tourism and understanding why they shouldnât do that.â Even so, human-wildlife conflict is still a problem. Elephants ramble into gardens and cheetahs kill the occasional goat, but the overall opinion of locals is shifting, especially as the Namibian government signals support for conservation thatâs more in step with local interests. âNamibiaâs communities already help look after lions, elephants, rhinos, water, plants and open land,â Rob Moffett explained a few days later, soon after I arrived at my third and final destination in northwest Namibia. âInstead of saying, âGood luck finding money every year,â the Namibia for Life fund says, âHere is a proper money box, a rule book, and a team to help you keep protecting nature.ââ Moffett is the general manager of sales and marketing at Ongava Game Reserve, a private stretch of savanna and mopane woodlands that stretches more than 74,000 acres next to Etosha National Park, one of the countryâs biggest visitor attractions. Itâs also the site of another positiveâand long overdueâstory of change. To reach it, I rented a gas-electric hybrid car from ATI Holidays and drove east from the Hoanib Valley. This type of travel is still popular in Namibia, with strong infrastructure supporting visitors. After a detailed briefing with an ATI staff member, I was kitted out with a folder packed with maps, a Namibian cell phone pre-programmed with key contacts, and a first-aid kit. I drove for several hours, listening to music and watching the desert scenery flash by. But driving solo can be tiring, and I was glad for the air travel between previous camps, seamlessly arranged by the Explorations Company. For US travelers unaccustomed to driving on the left side of the road, and often juggling a few shorter vacations, brief single-engine flights from camp to camp are increasingly preferred by high-end resorts opening in the northwest. The new Horizon by Ongava, where I had arrived, is one of those. Consisting of just three hilltop villas, the property debuted from renovations and a name reset in April 2026, and prioritizes seclusion and comfort. My accommodations unfolded in a graceful series of rooms with couches, a four-poster bed, and a dual-vanity bathroom. Outside, overlooking a plain of the greenest scenery Iâd seen so far, a wide deck hugged the hillside, and included two dining spaces, an outdoor shower, and a private plunge pool. My favorite touch was the large bench in the walk-in dressing room, carved in the shape of a servalâa wild cat native to sub-Saharan Africa. The dining, led by chef Festus Ilyambo, is a feat in its own right. That evening, in the open-air lounge, I asked Ilyambo for the recipes behind his potato pavÃ©âthinly sliced, buttery potatoes infused with organic thyme and fresh cream, then sautÃ©ed with garlicâand filet mignon, served with a jus and cognac sauce. The next morning, longtime guide Pascalis Kazimbu led me on a private walking safari in Ongava Game Reserve, pointing out everything from lilac-breasted rollers to white rhino mothers with calves tottering close behind and wildebeest that bleatedââgnuu, gnuuâ. Later that afternoon we set out on a game drive, pausing at a watering hole for sundowner drinks as dusk began to settle. I was sipping a local Tafel lager in the safari vehicle when a deep, reverberating roar sounded behind me, vibrating in my bones. Moments later, a male lion strolled out of the thin trees behind me, settling by the pond for a drink. With game viewing like this, verdant Ongava and its neighboring Etosha National Park are a welcome coda to the scenes of desert and dunes Iâd left behind. The circular route of my trip is a popular one: travelers arrive into the capital of Windhoek, travel in a rough circle that begins with awe-inspiring desert and ends near Etosha, and then head back to Windhoek to begin their journey home. But a coming Ongava project will add a new element for curious travelers. In 2024, the Indigenous San (or Bushmen) Hai//om community and Ongava agreed to a legally binding agreement to partner to manage a new concession, including a new lodge, on the southeast border of Etosha National Park. Slated to open in 2028, the new reserve will secure thousands of acres of land, strengthening wildlife corridors and helping to protect an important waterway called the !Gobaob Spring, where black rhinos and many other species gather to drink in the dry season. âThat place is a miracle,â Ongava manager Moffett said. âIn the Hai//omâs oral history, itâs the one spring that has never failed in their entire existence.â The implications of this new initiative, called the Ongava-Hai//om Joint Venture, extend far beyond wildlife. The concession carries profound historical significance because it includes part of the ancestral homeland of the Hai//om people, who were forcibly removed from Etosha by the government in the 1950s. âToday, most Hai//om people are living scattered on the outside of the park, but this is their home,â Moffett said. âFor them to reclaim management and ownership of this concession has the potential to become one of the most special community conservation stories of our time.â When the 25-year joint venture ends in 2049, the entire business will transfer from its current shared management to the Hai//om community. By protecting endangered wildlife while empowering the Hai//om people to build long-term prosperity, the new concession promises benefits for all involved, including visitors. Learning about this project felt like an encapsulation of everything Iâd seen and heard on this journey in northwest Namibia, where community-focused conservation held hands with high-end hospitality. I thought back to the rhino Iâd seen in my first days here, and the slow but steady work locals like Karutjaiva are doing to protect the species from the knifeâs edge of extinction. In Namibia, the stakes are high, but so is the promise of a more prosperous, wild future. Northern Namibia is one of our Best Places to Go in 2026. Find our full guide here.

item.title: This Italian island was voted the second best in Europe in Condé Nast Traveller's Readers' Choice Awards
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
When it comes to idyllic Mediterranean islands, it's not surprising to see the constant battle between Italy, Greece and Spain. Last year, Greece took the first position with the gorgeous island of Naxos, but Crete, Corfu, Rhodes, Skiathos, Mykonos, Folegandros and Santorini were also in the top twenty â meaning that the country of Socrates occupied nearly half of the list. This year, Greece has dominated the list once again. But while Naxos is still in the top three, it lost first place and dropped to third place, while other islands have made their debut. For 2026, the best island in Europe in this year's Readers' Choice Awards is Hydra, a serene, car-free island close to Athens. Sifnos, Paros, Santorini, Mykonos and Crete â as well as Naxos â are the other Greek islands in the list. Although Greece still got the top spot, Italy managed to sneak onto the podium, earning a well-deserved second place with Sardinia, as well as a fifth place slot with Sicily. As an Italian, I'm saddened not to see some of the smaller islands around Sicily, like Favignana, Filicudi, and Alicudi â but there is always next year. Italy is blessed with so many beautiful islands that picking a favourite can feel almost treacherous, but it's easy to see how Sardinia managed to climb its way to the top. Crystal-clear waters, unique and flavourful cuisine, archaeological sites â Sardinia is all of this and more. For decades, some corners of this vast island have been for Italy what St Tropez is for France: one of the rich and famous' favourite playgrounds. But just like Ibiza is not just a party destination and St Tropez has more to it than its glamorous reputation, Sardinia has a lot more to offer than yacht spotting and lavish dinners. The island is still rough around the edges, having preserved its wild nature and ancient traditions, and is a perfect destination for those looking to immerse themselves in nature. If cove-hopping around the Gulf of Orosei, trekking and canyoning in Su Gorropu, and relaxing on the white sand beaches of San Teodoro sounds like something you might like, book your trip and get a taste of what it would be like to live in the Blue Zone. For Italians, like me, Sardinia has always felt almost like a foreign destination. While now budget airlines have democratised holidays on the island, when I was growing up, travelling to Sardinia was more arduous and expensive than holidaying elsewhere in Italy â something reserved for the elite. The island is still glamorous and attracts just as many of the rich and famous today, but people are discovering that there is more to this eclectic land than Porto Cervo and Costa Smeralda. A bit like Ibiza, Sardinia needs to be explored to be fully appreciated. A road trip is the best way to move around and reach the small inland villages, like the historic village of Santu Lussurgiu or Mamoiada. The latter is particularly interesting to visit during the winter for the festival of Sant'Antonio Abate, which marks the start of the spectacular Sardinian carnival â a unique experience to see the famous Mamuthones, mysterious traditional masked figures whose origins are thought to stretch back centuries. If you are going to the island looking for sun, Sardinia's beach season stretches well beyond the peak summer months and you can enjoy the coves with fewer crowds in spring and autumn â unmissable are Cala Coticcio, Cala Spinosa and Cala Mariolu.

item.title: Art Basel Paris 2026: the best things to do during, according to insiders
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Paris is a paradise for art lovers all year round, but every October the city takes things up a notch when Paris Art Week rolls around. Collectors, artists, curators and gallery owners descend on the French capital for Art Basel Paris, as a packed calendar of exhibitions, parties, pop-ups and collaborations spills far beyond the walls of the Grand Palais. This year, the fair returns from 23 to 25 October, but some of the most exciting events are happening elsewhere in the city. From grand Parisian hotels transforming their restaurants into immersive works of art to underground clubs hosting all-night performances, there's plenty to discover, whether you're a serious collector or simply looking to experience a different side of Paris. But with so much happening across the capital, it's hard to know where to start. We've rounded up some of the most interesting events taking place during Art Basel Paris 2026 and asked the people behind them to share their own insider recommendations, from favourite neighbourhood restaurants and bars to the exhibitions they wouldn't miss. Where is Art Basel Paris held? Art Basel Paris 2026 takes place at the Grand Palais, one of the French capital's most iconic exhibition venues, located on Avenue Winston Churchill in the 8th arrondissement, just off the Champs-Élysées. The fair runs from Friday 23 to Sunday 25 October 2026, opening daily from 11am to 7pm. However, exhibitions, installations and special events will also take place across the city throughout Paris Art Week. How much do tickets to Art Basel Paris 2026 cost? Standard day tickets for Art Basel Paris 2026 cost €47 (£39), with reduced admission available for students and visitors under 26 for €30 (£25). An evening ticket for Friday 23 October, valid from 5pm to 7pm, costs €40 (£33), while a permanent pass is priced at €130 (£109). Tickets for the opening Vernissage on Thursday 22 October cost €120 (£100). Tickets can be purchased through the official Art Basel website. Can the public visit Art Basel Paris for free? While admission to the main Art Basel fair at the Grand Palais requires a ticket, visitors can enjoy plenty of art for free. The fair's official Public Program includes free exhibitions, installations and performances across Paris, including works displayed in public spaces and cultural institutions. Visitors can also attend the fair's Conversations programme for free with advance reservation, making it possible to experience much of the excitement of Art Basel without purchasing a ticket. Art Basel Paris 2026: the events worth knowing about Discover Chiharu Shiota's art at Shangri-La Paris Discover Chiharu Shiota's art at Shangri-La Paris Shangri-La Paris is hosting an exhibition by Japanese artist Chiharu Shiota from 14 to 27 October. Best known for her large-scale installations made from intricate networks of thread, Shiota explores themes of memory, identity, absence and human connection through her work. The exhibition offers visitors a chance to discover her artistic universe in the rather unexpected surroundings of one of Paris's most glamorous hotels, housed in the former residence of Prince Roland Bonaparte. And the best part? It's completely free to visit, whether you're staying at the hotel or simply passing through the city during Art Week. Anthony Schmitt, head concierge at Shangri-La Paris, says: “In our arrondissement, the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris offers an exceptional collection spanning some of the most influential artistic movements of the 20th and 21st centuries. We also recommend a visit to La Galerie Dior, where the story of one of Paris’s most iconic fashion houses unfolds, and the outdoor art installations along Avenue Winston Churchill.” If there's one place to experience Paris's creative nightlife during Art Basel, it's Silencio. The legendary private club, originally designed by filmmaker David Lynch, is hosting five nights of art, music and performances from 20 to 24 October. Curated by Sam Ozer, who has worked with MoMA and MoMA PS1 and founded the arts organisation TONO, Silencio Art Week brings together film screenings, artist conversations, live performances and DJ sets, blurring the lines between an exhibition and a night out. The programme also includes an exhibition of Kayode Ojo's nightlife photography, presented with Sweetwater gallery. Each evening kicks off at 7.30pm with artist screenings and conversations, followed by live performances at 10pm and DJ sets from 11pm, with names including Space Afrika, Avalon Emerson, Guy Gerber and Âme on the programme. It's an opportunity to experience a more underground side of Paris Art Week, far removed from the polished surroundings of the Grand Palais. Art and food have always made a rather wonderful pairing, but Le Meurice is taking things a step further this Art Basel. From 20 to 25 October, artist and designer Harry Nuriev is transforming the hotel's elegant Le Dalí restaurant into an immersive installation called The Stage, centred around its dining table. The experience includes six intimate dinners, each welcoming just 24 guests, with a ten-course menu created by chefs Alain Ducasse and Amaury Bouhours in response to Nuriev's artistic vision. But you don't necessarily have to book one of the exclusive dinners to experience the installation. Throughout the week, The Stage will also provide the backdrop for breakfast, lunch and afternoon tea, offering visitors the chance to experience contemporary art in a unique way. Experience 24 hours of art and techno at FVTVR Techno pioneer Richie Hawtin and contemporary artist John Gerrard are joining forces for an ambitious 24-hour event at the Institut du Monde Arabe. Beginning at midday on 24 October, the experience opens with INFIN.1.IRIDESCENT.STREAM, a digital installation by Gerrard accompanied by an original sound composition from Plastikman, Hawtin's musical alter ego. The exhibition is free to attend and begins with a conversation between the two artists, moderated by Marc Spiegler. At midnight, the event transforms into a 12-hour party curated by Hawtin, with DJ sets from Matador, Courtesy, Kristin Velvet and Reece Pritchard. Gerrard's work continues throughout the night with SPIRITS, an installation and live performance featuring Ana Osj. It's a chance to experience contemporary art in an entirely different setting, with the music carrying on until midday on Sunday. Experience Art Basel at Le Royal Monceau – Raffles Paris With its own art concierge, a collection of contemporary works and a private cinema, the hotel has established a strong connection to the arts. This year, it is also an official hotel partner of Art Basel Paris, welcoming participants in the fair's Conversations programme and providing a meeting place for artists, collectors and visitors throughout the week. Its restaurants and iconic Bar Long will be among the places where the art world gathers between exhibitions, making it a particularly interesting stop for those looking to soak up the atmosphere beyond the Grand Palais. Even if you're not staying overnight, there's always the option of stopping by for a drink. Step into Miles Aldridge's colourful world at Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme If you're a fan of photography, make sure to stop by Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, which is celebrating Art Basel with an exhibition dedicated to British fashion photographer Miles Aldridge. Running from 19 October to 1 December, Entrances and Exits / Entrées et Sorties brings together some of his most recognisable works. Known for his cinematic compositions, vibrant colours and carefully staged scenes, Aldridge has a distinctive style that blurs the boundaries between fashion photography and fine art. Curated by Constance Breton, the exhibition takes over the hotel's public spaces, including its lobby, corridors and Café Jeanne, transforming the five-star property into an unexpected gallery. The exhibition is free to visit, while a separate experience, 15 Minutes of Fame, gives a select number of guests the opportunity to have their Polaroid portrait taken by the photographer himself between 20 and 22 October. Discover Rocco Ritchie's paintings at Pierre Augustin Rose For Art Basel Paris 2026, French design house Pierre Augustin Rose is presenting an exhibition dedicated to British-American artist – and Madonna's son – Rocco Ritchie at its Galerie Hérold space in the 1st arrondissement. Born in 2000 and trained at Central Saint Martins and the Royal Drawing School in London, Ritchie is known for his figurative paintings and drawings, which draw inspiration from 20th-century British and European art and explore themes of memory, observation and personal experience. Rather than displaying his work in a traditional white-walled gallery, Pierre Augustin Rose has chosen to exhibit the paintings alongside its furniture and decorative objects, creating an intimate, domestic setting where contemporary art and design come together. It's an interesting opportunity to discover the young artist's work while exploring how paintings can transform, and be transformed by, the spaces they inhabit. Discover Alice Diop's immersive installation with Miu Miu For the third consecutive year, Italian fashion house Miu Miu is joining Art Basel Paris's public programme, this time with Geste de Consolation, an immersive installation by French filmmaker Alice Diop. Taking over the Palais d'Iéna from 21 to 25 October, the project marks Diop's first venture into the world of exhibitions, bringing together film, photography, sculpture, poetry, dance, music and performance. Featuring works by internationally acclaimed Black female artists, including photographer Zanele Muholi and sculptor Simone Leigh, the installation explores themes of representation, identity and healing through a combination of different artistic disciplines. It's an opportunity to discover a different side of the filmmaker's work, while experiencing one of the most interesting collaborations between fashion and contemporary art taking place during Paris Art Week. The exhibition is open to the public, with reservations available through the Miu Miu website. Admire Tracey Emin's monumental sculptures British artist Tracey Emin is taking over two locations in Paris for this year's Art Basel, bringing her deeply personal and expressive work to both a traditional gallery setting and the streets of the French capital. At White Cube Paris, an exhibition of new paintings and small-scale bronze sculptures offers visitors a closer look at the artist's exploration of the human experience, while three monumental sculptures – I lay here for you (2018), I Followed You to the End (2024) and I Will Not Be Alone (2025) – are on display outdoors at the Parvis des Droits de l'Homme, in front of the Cité de l'architecture et du patrimoine. Exploring themes of vulnerability, resilience and transformation through the human body, the sculptures offer a chance to experience the work of one of Britain's most celebrated contemporary artists without stepping inside a gallery. The outdoor installation will remain on display until 1 November 2026.

item.title: Capital One Venture X Business review: High earning rates and premium perks for businesses
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The Capital One Venture X Business is a compelling choice for collecting rewards on all business-related purchases and enjoying top-tier travel perks — all for a reasonable annual fee. If you're a business owner looking for a fixed-rate rewards card to maximize multiple types of spending, few cards on the market are as straightforward. However, you'll want to factor in whether you'd rather maximize bonus categories or receive more business-related perks. If so, you may be better off with another business card. But with useful travel benefits and consistent earning rates, I see the Venture X Business as a great option for many. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐½ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. The Venture X Business is Capital One's top-tier travel rewards business card, earning transferable Capital One miles on purchases and providing solid benefits for cardholders. If you're familiar with the personal Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, the business version is essentially identical in terms of earning and benefits. The Venture X Business card's perks include airport lounge access and an annual $300 credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel. The card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on most purchases, with a pair of bonus categories that only apply to certain purchases made within the Capital One Business Travel portal. You can redeem the miles you earn to offset travel purchases at a 1 cent per mile value, or you can potentially unlock more value by leveraging one of Capital One's 15-plus transfer partners. These perks come for a $395 annual fee — modest considering the card's competition. For a $395 annual fee, don't expect a long list of statement credits and extra benefits. However, the Venture X Business still provides excellent perks for business travelers. These two benefits effectively offset the Venture X Business' annual fee on their own. The annual travel credit reduces the effective annual fee to $95 by slashing $300 off any booking made through Capital One Business Travel, the issuer's business travel portal. I'd recommend using this statement credit for boutique hotel stays, car rentals or flights. The Venture X Business also provides 10,000 bonus miles each year, beginning on your first anniversary. TPG's October 2026 valuations place the value of these miles at $185. When you pair that value with the $300 travel credit, you receive $485 in total value, which more than offsets the card's annual fee. Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee statement credit Venture X Business cardholders receive up to $120 toward TSA PreCheck or Global Entry application fees. If you already have a card with this benefit, this perk is still useful. That's because you can use this credit for anyone as long as you pay the fee with your Venture X Business. The Venture X Business provides access to Capital One's issuer lounge network. These lounges are located at: Cardholders can also visit Capital One Landings, which offer a dining-focused alternative to traditional airport lounges, at: You can also add up to four authorized users with lounge access for $125 per year each. Primary cardholders can bring up to two guests to Capital One lounges and one guest to Capital One Landings for free after spending at least $75,000 on their card in a calendar year. You'll also receive unlimited access to 1,300-plus Priority Pass lounges worldwide for you and up to two guests. There are multiple additional benefits cardholders can enjoy, including access to Capital One’s Premier Collection and Lifestyle Collection hotels. You'll also receive various travel and shopping protections, including: - Ride-hailing protection (a unique benefit that includes coverage for covered property incidents, accidental death and accidental medical events while using ride-hailing services) Business-related benefits on the Venture X Business include the ability to add employee cards for no additional cost (lounge access costs $125 each), access to itemized spending reports and no preset spending limits (which means you have to pay your bill in full each month). Finally, this is a great card to use abroad since it charges no foreign transaction fees. The simple earning structure on the Venture X Business means you won’t have to worry about whether your purchase falls in a bonus-earning category. You’ll earn: - 10 miles per dollar spent on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel (18.5% return based on TPG's valuations) - 5 miles per dollar spent on flights and vacation rentals purchased through Capital One Business Travel (9.25% return) - 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases (3.7% return) However, if you spend a significant portion of your business budget in specific areas such as shipping and advertising, you may find the lack of business-related bonus categories to be limiting. You'll usually get the best value out of your miles when you transfer them to any of Capital One’s 15-plus airline and hotel partners. However, you can also redeem your miles simply at a flat rate of 1 cent per mile. Redemption examples include booking travel through Capital One Business Travel, redeeming miles as a statement credit to cover travel purchases and purchasing gift cards. Carly Helfand, TPG's director of site strategy, once redeemed 100,000 Capital One miles to take $1,000 off a last-minute Airbnb stay. The most valuable redemption option for your miles is to transfer them to a Capital One travel partner. You have 15-plus hotel and airline programs to choose from, including Air Canada Aeroplan, Choice Privileges and Singapore KrisFlyer. I like to leverage SkyTeam alliance partners when transferring my Capital One miles. Last year, I transferred 15,000 miles to Air France-KLM Flying Blue (and paid $35 in taxes and fees) for two one-way domestic tickets from Greenville-Spartanburg International Airport (GSP) in South Carolina to Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) on Delta Air Lines for a wedding. Where the Venture X Business could fall short The Venture X Business may not be the best choice for every business owner. Here are some downsides worth considering: - Capital One's issuer lounge footprint is smaller than some of its competitors. - The $300 annual travel credit is limited to Capital One Business Travel purchases. - There are no additional statement credits to maximize beyond the annual travel credit. (This could be a positive for cardholders who dislike "coupon-heavy" cards.) - There are no business-related bonus categories, which may deter business owners who often spend in one specific area (such as advertising or general travel). However, if you value simplicity and would prefer not to pay a sky-high annual fee, it would make sense to choose the Venture X Business as your travel rewards business card. As mentioned previously, it's natural to compare the Venture X Business card to the personal Venture X card, as the two provide almost identical perks and earning rates. However, there are two key considerations to weigh. The Venture X Business provides business perks, such as itemized spending reports, and the card's balance must be paid in full every month, since it has no preset spending limit. This is not the case with the personal Venture X. When to apply for the Venture X Business New Venture X Business applicants can earn up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit after meeting two spending thresholds: - Earn 150,000 bonus miles after spending $40,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. - Earn an additional 150,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 Capital One Business Travel credit (to use in the first cardholder year) after spending $120,000 total on purchases in the first four months from account opening. According to TPG's valuations, the full offer is worth up to $6,550 (including the $1,000 travel credit). While this isn't the highest bonus we've seen in the card's history, it's still a competitive offer that exceeds our recommended threshold for when to apply.
