item.title: The Golden Rules of Airplane Etiquette—Because We Have Simply Seen Enough
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
It is my firm belief that everyoneâno matter their age, gender, race, or Delta SkyMiles Medallion Statusâneeds to learn proper airplane etiquette, and the earlier the better. As a freelance travel writer, I get on lots of flights to and from different parts of the world, and Iâve seen the same silly mistakes, rude behavior, and even downright harmful stunts enacted by all types of travelers. But by that same token, Iâve also witnessed acts of generosity and helpfulness that all people universally appreciate. So what, exactly, are the rules at 35,000 feet? To draft such a constitution, I tapped three of CondÃ© Nast Travelerâs Top Travel Specialists who are experts in air travel, in addition to my own first-hand experience: Sophie Caulcutt, co-founder of The Voyager Club; Vikram Seshadri, co-founder of In Residence; and Paul Tumpowsky, chief revenue officer of Fora. And to get the real insider take on how we should behave in the air, I spoke with two working flight attendants: Rich Henderson, a flight attendant for a US-based airline and co-host of the podcast Two Guys on A Plane; and a US-based flight attendant and content creator (@lifeinlayovers on TikTok) named Liam. In general, we agreed that thereâs no environment where etiquette (or the lack thereof) matters more than when youâre sitting shoulder-to-shoulder with dozens of other seatbelt-strapped passengers inside a metal tube hurling through the skies. And while commercial air travel may not always be kind to us, we can choose to be part of the solution. As Tumpowsky of Fora pleads,: âPerhaps we can look inside ourselves to make the overall traveling experience better for us and our fellow travelers.â In the spirit of doing unto others as we would have them do unto us, below are the golden rules of airplane etiquette. Keep these principles and good habits in mind, and youâll find that, even when everyone else around you is behaving badly, youâll feel all the better for being a kind and considerate traveler. A true professional, some may even go so far to say. Boarding last is chic (if you can) Among travelers, especially those seated in economy, no one is dying to spend more time on the plane than they have to. So instead of crowding the gateâa rookie move that will earn you the unattractive nickname of âgate liceââbe patient and wait to board last. Your assigned seat will still be there at the end of boarding. (After all, a queen is never late. Everyone else is simply early.) Jostling to get on board early to secure overhead bin space? The crew will almost always find a spot, even if itâs not directly above your seat; or theyâll check your bag into the hold at no extra cost. To mitigate the inconvenience, pack light and put together your âseat bagâ so you have all your essentials (more on these points below). Are you flying in business or first class? Fabulous. âLinger in the lounge, enjoy the restaurant, and board last,â says Seshadri of In Residence. âYour overhead bin space is dedicated and waiting for you.â For parents traveling with kids, you might actually want to be among the last passengers to board. âWhy spend an extra 30 or 40 minutes sitting on a plane with young children if you donât have to?â Tumpowsky says. âBut I completely understand why new parents, in particular, may want to board early to make sure they have enough storage within reach for everything theyâll need during a long flight.â Pack your âseat bag,â and do it before boarding Make your personal item count: Before getting on the plane, prepare a âseat bagâ that contains all your in-flight must-haves and keep it close to you in your seat. For me, thatâs usually my fanny pack with my passport, boarding pass, phone, AirPods, eye mask, lip balm, hand cream, phone charger, and battery pack. Maybe my Kindle or a copy of The New Yorker; a toothbrush and toothpaste for overnight flights. This will eliminate or reduce the need to rummage through the bag under the seat in front of you, or step out into the aisle to reach for your luggage in the overhead bins. Turns out, doing this is also helpful for the people around you, according to Henderson of Two Guys on a Plane: âBoarding is basically a giant traffic jam, and one person standing in the aisle reorganizing their entire suitcase can hold up a hundred people behind them. Have what you need for the flight ready before you board, find your seat, put your bag away, and step out of the aisle as quickly as possible.â Boardâand deboardâefficiently and graciously First off, acknowledge the flight attendants when you board with eye contact, a smile, a quick hello. These are the people here to make sure you stay safe on the plane and everything goes smoothly, first and foremost. Be a good human and treat them with the dignity they deserve, and youâll get the same treatment in kind. At the end of the flight, do the same thing and thank the crewâyou all made it! Next, carry-on bags. People tend to overpack heavy carry-on bags because most US airlines do not weigh them, explains Liam of @lifeinlayovers, so boarding becomes even more hectic and slow when you canât lift your own stuff into the overhead bins. Try to pack only what you can literally carry. Consider too your own physical abilities, height, and strength, and pack accordingly. And if you see someone struggling with putting away their carry-ons and you can help, do so. It helps everyone out, and makes the boarding process go more smoothly. The flight attendants will thank you. Speaking of: Note that many airlines discourage flight attendants from helping with your overhead luggage because of the risk of injury, says Henderson, so donât expect that every FA can or will lend you a hand. While weâre on the topic of overhead bins, Henderson says, âPlease donât put your small purse or jacket in the overhead bin when people are still looking for space for their actual suitcases.â Save putting them away in the overhead space until boarding is mostly complete; there will always be space on the plane for your stuff, Liam says. As for deboarding the plane, a few more best practices: Do not get into the aisle while the plane is still taxiing to the gate. Once the plane comes to a complete stop, thatâs when deboarding can begin. Wait for the rows in front of you to get up and head to the exit, rather than scrambling to snatch your items from the overhead bins and just crowding the aisle. As space opens up in the aisle, thatâs when you stand up, get your bags, and exit. Itâs possible someone behind you will react exasperated, believing you should have gotten your stuff earlierâwhen there was no room to do so. If that happens, give them a smile (or a sly wink, if youâre feeling cheeky), and retrieve your luggage calmly, knowing that youâre in the right. If you have a tight connection, inform a flight attendant When youâre transiting and have limited time to get from Flight A to Flight B, kindly inform a flight attendant prior to landing. âI believe the appropriate protocol is to speak with a flight attendant rather than attempt to negotiate your way to the front of the aircraft,â Tumpowsky says. âThe crew can assess just how tight your connection really is, determine whether special consideration is warranted, and, if appropriate, make an announcement asking other passengers to remain seated. That request carries considerably more authority coming from the flight crew than from a passenger who has decided that their connection is more important than everyone elseâs.â Caulcutt of The Voyager Club agrees, saying that the crew may even consider it essential to move your seat closer to the exitâor at least closer to the aisleâif your connection is extremely tight or if they anticipate a delayed arrival. When approaching the crew, Caulcutt says, âI often find that a trip to the galley, during boarding or shortly after, to politely explain the situation one-on-one works best.â When someone asks you to swap seats, itâs OK to say no(!) My seat, my choice! When we select our seats on a plane, especially when we pay to get assigned places or use status benefits to do so, we are well within our rights to keep it. Able-bodied spouses, families, and friends can reunite after the flight. You can politely and firmly refuse to swap. (Exercise caution if using the correct but risky phrase: âYour lack of planning is not my problem.â) âBut just apply common sense,â says Caulcutt. âYou don't want to separate an elderly couple,â who may physically need each other for assistance, or âa mother from a weeping child.â Because did you really want to sit next to that wailing five year old anyway? Swap with the parent who can calm them down. If youâre feeling chatty, read the roomâor rather, the metal tube Some of us love making friends wherever we go, but when youâre going to be stuck on a plane with hundreds of other people in a steel projectile hurtling through the air, the rules of social engagement get a touch more delicate. So whatâs acceptable, and where do you draw the line? âA brief conversation and a little cordiality are perfectly appropriate,â says Tumpowsky. Itâs not a bad idea, though by no means required, to establish some rapport with those around youâbut donât force anything. âIf your seatmate engages and the feeling is mutual, by all means, enjoy the conversation,â Tumpowsky continues. âBut no one should feel obligated to continue a conversation longer than they're comfortable with. A polite exchange of pleasantries is not a binding commitment to discuss your respective life stories until the landing gear is employed.â If youâre traveling with a friend or friends and youâre all prone to yapping, keep a few things in mind: âKeep the tone of the conversation low,â says Caulcutt. âPeople in planes tend to talk louder than they realize because of engine noise. Try to keep your voice at a level that your seatmate can hear comfortably but the rows around you canât easily follow.â Try to keep topics light and disagreements to a minimum, she adds. If you get into a fight, you wonât have much room to put some distance between you on a plane. And on night or red-eye flights, the lights in the cabin are usually dimmed and people are trying to sleep, Caulcutt says, so keep conversations to a whisper whenever possible. Otherwise, save them for later on the ground. Speaking of: When babies cry, have some compassion Be patient, and take deep breaths. âNo one hates it more than the parents,â says Caulcutt. Period! Watch the safety demoâjust to be nice, if nothing else OK, well, it really is for our own safety in the air. As Henderson says, âI promise we flight attendants are not doing the safety demonstration for our own entertainment!â Do as advised and check where your nearest exits are; and see where the closest bathroom is, while youâre at it. Brush up on the brace position appropriate for the cabin youâre in. Enjoy the safety video, if there is one (the Philippine Airlines âSafetynovela,â depicted as a soap opera, is my current favorite). If the FAs are doing a live demo, give them your attention and a smile. This is all the more important when youâre seated in an exit row. When the FAs check in with you about the responsibilities you have in the case of an emergency, answer truthfully regarding whether or not you're physically, mentally, or even spiritually able to carry out what needs to be done. This is the cost of the exit-row legroom. (Also, the exit-row legroom comes with the price of not being able to stow luggage in front of you, as thereâs no seat to keep them under, so bear that in mind when picking your place on the plane.) Fasten your seatbelt whenever youâre seated. Really The fasten-your-seatbelt sign is not a suggestion. âTurbulence can happen without warning, even when the sky looks perfectly clear,â Henderson says. Liam explains that the flight deck turns on the sign when there's a forecast of bad weather up ahead, either from radar or aircraft ahead of the plane youâre on. So keep your belt fastened whenever youâre seated, Seshadri says, âeven if loosely! Youâll never regret it.â Go ahead and recline your seat, but donât be a jerk about it All our experts and FAs agree that reclining your seat is fair game. Thatâs what itâs there for. As Tumpowsky says, âWhether itâs the overhead light, window shade, or reclining, I generally believe you have the right to use the product as it was designed.â And everyone is also on the same page when it comes to meal time: Donât do it while the person behind you is eating. Itâs just good manners. âA little courtesy goes a long way,â Seshadri says. âRecline slowly, be mindful if the person behind you is using itâlike working on a laptopâand put your seat upright when the crew asks, especially for takeoff and landing.â On a plane, as in life: Be considerate of others. Go ahead and use the call button, but again, donât be a jerk about it This is another point on which all our experts were in agreement. The flight attendant call button is absolutely there to be used, especially if you need assistance, have a medical concern, or thereâs something that requires a crew memberâs attentionâlike if your phone fell into the cracks of the seat. (A very real concern! If the machinery ends up cracking your phone and the battery leaks, it could be a fire hazard.) âBut if the FAs are visibly in the middle of beverage service and you just want another soda, itâs usually easier to ask us when we reach your row,â Henderson says. And donât use the button to summon them every five minutes for things that can wait. There are sometimes hundreds of other passengers and only a few of them. Liam says, âStaffing has decreased and cabins have expanded. Please be patient with us, especially when weâre busy with service or thereâs turbulence.â Give the middle armrests to the unlucky person in the middle seat Again, among our experts, this is a universally acknowledged truth: âThe middle seat passenger deserves both middle armrests,â Henderson says. After all, the window passenger gets the window, and the aisle passenger gets a little extra breathing room. âThe poor person in the middle deserves something!â he says. (Liam agrees: âAs someone who often gets the middle seat when flying standby on benefits, please, for the love of all things good, give me both middle armrests.â) âNo bare feet on display ever!â Caulcutt says. And rightly so. You can remove your shoes, especially on long-haul flights; our feet do swell in flight. Keep your socks on (try compression socks); swiftly and discreetly swap into a fresh pair if youâve lost the ability to smell yourself. Do not ever prop your feet up on the armrests, seatbacks, or tray tables. (Quick trick: Use your backpack or duffel bag, under the seat in front of you, as a foot rest.) Hendersonâs advice: âNever walk into an airplane bathroom barefoot or even just in socks. That mysterious liquid on the floor is probably not water.â And Seshadriâs: âPlease never clip your toenails or file them on a flight!â Do not take calls in-flight, and do wear headphones for music and movies For better or worse, Wi-Fi connectivity is getting better on planes, meaning that what often used to be a relatively quiet airborne sanctuary is now another space in which the cacophony of modern life can invade. So, again, donât be a jerk about it. Our experts agree that headphones and earbuds are a must, whether youâre listening to music, watching a movie on your own device, or scrolling through Instagram Reels. Do not take your high-level meeting from 35,000 feet in the air. âVoice and video calls are usually prohibited by airline policy or regulations,â Henderson says. âAn airplane is a shared space, not your personal living room or office.â Expect these principles to be sticking points in the coming years. âHigh-bandwidth internetâand potentially the ability to make calls more easily in the airâis going to create the next battleground in flight etiquette,â Tumpowsky says. âJust because technology allows you to do something doesnât necessarily mean 200 other passengers want you to do it.â Alas, from personal experience, it has to be said! And think about your surroundings when youâre watching a movie and thereâs a graphic scene in the story, whether sexual or otherwise. Consider speeding through if there are, say, children around. That said, itâs really up to youâespecially if the movie or show in question is offered through the in-flight entertainment system. I was once on a flight watching an episode of And Just Like Thatâ¦ and they got to the infamous Snapple scene in Carrieâs apartment and, well, I didnât skip it since I was pretty much alone in the business class cabin. As long as youâre not doing a full-on downward dog in the aisle, Caulcutt says, stretching in the aisle is fine. Keep it quick and respectful. Do some standing spine twists, lymphatic taps, and gentle walking, then return to your seat. Donât do it during meal service or when the FAs are working. If an FA tells you to return to your seat, donât make a fuss and sit back down. âWe encourage passengers to get up and move around when itâs safe, especially on long flights, but the aisle is a workspace for flight attendants and an important pathway for everyone on board, especially in the event of an emergency where we must move quickly,â Henderson says. So donât block the aisle, congregate around the bathrooms, or interfere with the crew doing their jobs. âA little stretching is one thing, but turning the plane into a yoga studio is another,â he says. Yes, itâs OK to gently wake your neighbor when you need to go to the bathroom Thereâs nothing wrong with politely waking someone if you need to get out of your row to reach the toilet. Just be considerate (there it is again, basic kindness). Liam says, âIâd hate to be woken up after Iâve just gotten comfortable; for me, thatâs having an eye mask and headphones on. Watch out for those signs. But if you have to go, you have to go.â Wake someone up the way youâd want to be woken: Respectfully. The flip side is that if someone in your row gets up to use the bathroom and disturbs you, it might be a good opportunity for you to go as well. âThink of it as airplane efficiency,â Tumpowsky says. âYou may save everyone another round of climbing over one another later in the flight.â By the way, do not get out of your seat by using the seat in front of you as a handle Whether they physically need to or not, many people allow their intrusive thoughts to win and grab the top of the seat in front of them to pull themselves up. This is awful and rude. If you really need support, Tumpowsky says, âthe proper etiquette is to use your own row of seats for support whenever possible. Pulling on the seat in front of you can jolt the person sitting thereâand if theyâre sleeping, youâve just unnecessarily woken them up.â In the bathroom, wipe down any spills and remember to flush the toilet I was gonna say, âleave the bathroom the way you leave yours,â but the mileage may vary on that one. Keep the place tidy, wipe anything you made wet as a courtesy to the person who comes in after you, and dispose of any waste properly, as the laws of common decency intend. âJust because you donât want to push down the flap to discard your trash doesnât mean you can just start a pile of it on the ground or counter,â Liam says. âAnd for the love of aviation, wear shoes in there!â Henderson adds. Forget everything you heard about dressing well for an upgrade Maybe there was once a time, in a faraway land, when dressing nicely for a flight might have improved your chances of an upgrade. No longer. âToday, upgrades are much more likely to be determined by status, algorithms, bidding, or other systems, so I donât think your wardrobe is moving you up the list,â Tumpowsky says. âDress comfortably. Being comfortable will have a much bigger impact on your flight experience than looking like you belong in first class.â Instead, dress well because you respect yourself You can do so comfortably! May I interest you in a cashmere jogger set or a wrinkle-free traveling suit? Figure out a travel uniform that works for youâsomething comfortable that also makes you feel put-together. Itâs a proven fact (by me, anecdotally) that looking good helps you feel good, like you can handle any travel hiccup like flight delays or lost baggage with dignity and grace. But hey if itâs not your literal style, no one says you have to. âAlways be polite to the plane crew,â Caulcutt says. Flight attendants arenât responsible for the weather, delays, baggage fees, or most airline policies, so donât take your frustrations out on the people who are there to keep you safe and comfortable to the best of their abilities. Patience and kindness can go a long way, Henderson says, and Seshadri reminds everyone to extend that respect to the airport staff and your fellow passengers. Moving with respect and courtesy, he says, âwill earn you not just a better flight but a good dose of karma and happiness too.â Yes, cabins are getting stuffed with more seats, and those seats are getting smaller, while crew staffing keeps getting cut. And yet, even in the face of all this, on top of everything going on in our world, we get to travel. So itâs more important than ever to cultivate a sense of solidarity as travelers. As Liam puts it, âWeâre truly all in this metal tube together.â

item.title: How to Make Better Pie Crust, According to a Pastry Chef
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
There is a lot of subtlety that goes into making a good pie crust, the types of intuitive moves or small tips you pick up in a professional kitchen (or by baking with an experienced relative). But a few principles make all the difference: keeping the butter cold, avoiding overmixing, letting the dough rest, and baking the finished pie long enough. Below, and in my book A Good Bake, I cover the little things that matter, from making and rolling out pie dough to crimping the crust and knowing when a pie is done. These are the techniques I use to make delicious, professional-looking pies, no matter what recipe Iâm following. A pie is only as good as its crust. I use a few different recipes for pie crust, but my go-to pie dough is pÃ¢te brisÃ©e. BrisÃ©e means âbrokenâ in French, and in this dough, the butter is âbrokenâ into the flour, creating a layered, flaky crust. PÃ¢te sucrÃ©e, by contrast, means âsugar dough.â It contains sugar and egg and is prepared like a cookie dough, with the butter and sugar creamed together. In a professional bakery, cooks prepare pie dough up to several days in advance. Set yourself up the same way at home. Making the dough ahead gives it time to rest and chill, so itâs ready to roll when you need it. You can also freeze pie dough up to one month in advance; wrap it well and defrost it overnight in the fridge. The essential ingredients in pie dough are flour, water, a pinch of salt, maybe a very small amount of sugar, and some fat. Many traditional American pie dough recipes call for lard, rendered pork fat, which makes for an exceptionally flaky crust. I love lard, but quality lard is not always easy to find, so I use good old-fashioned unsalted butter for my pie and tart crusts. With good technique, you can achieve plenty of flakiness and get that great buttery flavor. Many pie recipes call for cutting the butter into Â¼" cubes. I prefer largish Â½" chunks. After cutting the butter into pieces, I arrange them onto a plate and freeze them for 10 minutes so the butter gets as cold as can be without turning rock solid. When mixed into the flour, some larger chunks remain intact. When you roll out the dough, those chunks form striations of butter. As the crust bakes, the water in the butter turns to steam, creating microscopic flaky layersâand a light, tender crust. Lots of recipes call for adding ice water to the dough. I find that cold water from my refrigerator (like from a water filter or door dispenser) works fine. That said, if you want to use super-chilled water, it certainly wonât hurt. Add water only after you mix the flour and butter. When the water joins the party, gluten starts to form. Too much gluten development toughens pie dough, making the finished crust heavy and dense rather than light and flaky. Mixing the flour with cold butter first coats the flourâs proteins, impeding the interaction between the water and the flour and reducing gluten development. You might be tempted to mix pie dough until it forms a homogeneous mass, like cookie dough. Resist. Mix only until the dough begins to come together. When you transfer the dough to the counter, it should still be a bit crumbly and shaggy, with small, observable chunks of butter. The dry bits will hydrate and come together as the dough rests. And on that note: After bringing the dough together, I shape it into a round disk or brick, depending on the shape Iâll roll it into. Then I wrap it in plastic wrap, run a rolling pin over it to compact and flatten it, and put it in the refrigerator to rest. A good rest lets the flour fully absorb any moisture so that the dough comes together completely. Resting the dough also relaxes the gluten, making it easier to roll out and less likely to shrink in the oven. If your kitchen runs warm, work quickly and give the dough extra time in the refrigerator whenever it starts to feel soft or tacky. You can also chill your mixing bowl, bench scraper, and rolling pin before you start. Take the dough out of the refrigerator, put it on the counter, and let it sit until it feels malleable but still firm (10 to 15 minutes) before rolling. The goal is for the dough to be just pliable enough to roll but not so soft that it starts to stick. Conversely, rolling our cold dough straight from the fridge can cause it to crack. In the meantime, clear space and have your rolling pin ready, along with anything else you might need, such as a bench knife, cookie cutter, straightedge, pastry wheel, knife, and flour (or, in some cases, sugar) for dusting your work surface. Whatever will happen to the dough after rolling, make sure those supplies are ready too: Line a baking sheet with parchment paper or have your pie pan ready so you can go right from rolling to assembly, no warming dough waiting on your counter. Once you start rolling, move quickly. Even the firmest dough block will soften quickly under the friction of the rolling pin and the heat of your hands. The whole process shouldnât take more than a minute or two. It may be unconventional, but I always butter a pie plate before arranging the dough. The butter helps hold the dough in place as I shape it and provides insurance for removing it from the pan after baking. I smear enough butter on the bottom and sloped sides of the plate to leave a visible layer. I usually use cold butter, but slightly softened also works. There are two ways to âlineâ a pie plateâthat is, to make sure the dough fits snugly inside. Either fold the dough in half, lift it from the surface you rolled it out on, and place it in the pan. Or roll the dough onto your rolling pin and carry it over on the pin. I fold the dough when lining a round pie plate, and I roll it onto a rolling pin when using a jelly roll pan, which requires a larger piece. Use whatever method you find easiest. In either case, carry the dough until it hovers over the pie plate, tart pan, jelly roll pan, or other vessel, centering it as much as you can. Then gently lay it onto the dish and unfold or unroll it. Adjust the dough so that itâs centered on the pan. Gently lift one edge of the dough with one hand and use the other to press it into the bottom of the pan, working your way around the perimeter. Use a delicate touch, and resist pulling the dough, which will cause it to spring back when baked and create thin spots in the crust. Next, gently run your finger along the rim to press the dough onto it, just enough to ensure it adheres. This allows you to see how much dough is overhanging. Make sure it is even all the way around and sitting nicely on top of the rim. Use kitchen shears to trim the overhanging dough so there is an even 1" hanging over the perimeter of the pie dish. (Discard the trimmings or smush them together into a disk and refrigerate or freeze the dough to make a pie another day.) If you are making a double-crust or lattice-topped pie, trim the top sheet of dough or lattice so it is flush with the outside edge of the pan. In pie making, âcrimpingâ means forming the decorative, wavy edge around the perimeter of a pie. To crimp, tightly roll the overhanging dough toward the center of the pie to form a thick lip that rests on the ridge of the plate. While many recipes call for folding the excess dough under, I prefer folding it up and over. When youâre finished, the dough shouldn't hang over the rim. The process is the same whether you are making a single- or double-crust pie. For a double crust, roll the bottom crust over the top crust, sealing the filling inside. As you form this ridge, use your fingers to shape the edge of the rolled crust so that it is rounded and even. Once the entire edge is rolled, place the index finger and thumb of one hand on the inside edge of the ridge and use the index finger of your other hand to push the outside edge toward the center of the pie, forming a V or U shape. Continue around the perimeter until you have crimped the entire crust. There is a lot of chilling when making pie. First, you chill the butter. Then you chill the finished dough before rolling it out. Youâll also want to chill the pie dish after lining it, and again after crimping and filling the dough, before baking. If youâve ever wondered why pies in professional bakeries look so much prettier than your homemade ones, itâs because they chill themâor even freeze themâbefore baking. Chilling the uncooked pie helps it hold its shape better during baking. In my kitchens, we often freeze a fully assembled fruit pie (overnight is best), then bake it directly from frozen. To bake a frozen pie, put it in the oven straight from the freezer and add 10 to 20 minutes to the total baking time, using the recipeâs visual indicators for doneness in the recipe. Always put a baking sheet under pies before baking. This is especially important with fruit pies, to prevent the bubbling fruit juices from spilling over the edge of the pan onto your oven floor. Also called pre- or par-baking, blind baking refers to baking the crust before adding the filling. For many custard pies, which cook faster than fruit pies, youâll partially blind-bake the crust to keep it from getting soggy or even staying raw. For pies and tarts whose fillings are not baked at all, youâll blind-bake the crust until itâs fully golden brown To blind-bake a crust, line the shaped, crimped, unbaked pie shell with parchment paper (crinkle the paper first to fit the pie shell better), then fill the parchment-lined dough with pie weights to prevent the crust from puffing while it bakes. BAâs favorite pie weights are inexpensive steel ball bearings, but many cooks use dried beans or rice; label any food items you use as âpie weightsâ when the pie is done, since they will not be good for cooking after baking. Depending on how cold the pie is when you put it in the ovenâand depending on your ovenâs hot spots and other quirksâbaking time can vary, so I always rely on the recipeâs visual cues for doneness. The crust should be a rich shade of golden brown. For a fruit pie, the filling must be bubbling through the lattice in the center of the pie or the vent cut into its top. If the filling isnât bubbling in the center (not just around the sides), the fruit hasnât cooked down enough. Remove it too early, and you risk a filling that weeps when you cut a slice. Custard pies must bake until they are set. A set custard will wobble slightly when you jiggle the pan, but it shouldnât slosh around like liquid. Avoid baking a custard pie so long that itâs fully set, which can cause surface cracks as the pie cools. Cooling time is essential to pie making. Custard pies need to set (and sometimes chill for several hours), and fruit pies need ample time to gel and firm. For beautiful slices that hold their shape, the wait is worthwhile. Why is my pie crust tough? Overmixing or overhandling the dough encourages gluten development, which can make the baked crust tough rather than tender. Mix only until the dough begins to come together; it should still look a little shaggy, with visible pieces of butter. Why did my pie crust shrink or slump? Pie dough can shrink if it hasnât rested long enough or if you stretch it while fitting it into the pan. Let the dough rest in the refrigerator before rolling, gently ease it into the pie plate without pulling, and chill the shaped crust again before baking. Slumped crusts can happen if you remove the pie weights too early or you donât fill the crust enough. Add weights to fill the crust to the rim of the pie dish, and donât remove them until the crust is set (it should look dry and the parchment will no longer stick). Why isnât my pie crust flaky? The butter may have gotten too warm or worked too thoroughly into the flour. For distinct flaky layers, keep the butter cold and leave some larger pieces intact. If the dough becomes soft or tacky while you're working, return it to the refrigerator until firm. Why does my pie dough crack when I roll it out? Dough thatâs too cold can crack when you roll it, while dough that hasnât hydrated enough may crumble. Let chilled dough sit until itâs pliable but still firm before rolling. If it remains dry and won't hold together, the problem may be insufficient hydration. Theyâll be here whenever you need them. item.title: Soothing Rice Porridge
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. Itâs what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking. If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which youâve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available. In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month itâs a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, Â¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (youâll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek). Step 2Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt. Step 3Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

item.title: Why More Women Are Traveling Abroad for Egg Freezing and IVF
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
My path to seeking reproductive healthcare outside the US began in the same way it would have at home: It started with life not going according to my neatly organized plan. In summer 2025, I found myself freshly divorced and looking out over the proverbial fertility cliff of turning 35. I suddenly felt the need to act fast. I was unsure about having children, but I wanted to keep that door open for the future. As a self-employed writer with health insurance that leaves much to be desired, I knew going abroad for a more affordable option was my only choiceâat least the only financially responsible one. Thatâs how I found myself in the office of Doctor Daniela Paz Cervantes, an OBGYN in Oaxaca, Mexico, who oversaw my care for two rounds of egg freezing just a few months later. Iâm not unique in my search for medical care abroad. Although exact numbers are difficult to track, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that âmillions of US residents travel internationally for medical care each year,â listing reproductive tourism as one of the main categories of services that they seek. While I went to Mexico for my treatments, Spain, Greece, Cyprus, and Barbados are also particularly popular for fertility tourism. Dr. Mario Vega Croker, Medical Director of Panama Fertility located in Panama City, Panama, has noticed more Americans knocking on his door. Panama Fertility opened nearly 40 years ago as a small clinic catering to local families; fast forward to today, and itâs grown into one of the most prolific clinics in Central America, with half of their patients hailing from the US and Caribbean. âAmerican patients are one of our fastest-growing groups, especially in gestational surrogacy, [receiving] egg donations, and IVF,â says Dr. Vega Croker. âMany come to us after putting their dreams on hold because treatment at home felt out of reach [â¦] Finding the same expertise and quality of care at about half the cost often gives them the chance to finally begin, or to try again.â According to FertilityIQ, a data-based fertility education platform, the average egg freezing cycle costs $16,000 in the US. Meanwhile, I spent about $7,000 for one round, which is inclusive of what I paid for flights, food, accommodations, and activities for the three weeks I was in Mexico for my treatment. And I appreciated the quality of my care: My entire cycle was incredibly thorough and personalized, even before I touched down in Oaxaca. It was a no-brainer. Alisa Purdie, a California-based online business coach, faced a similar set of choices when she got divorced at 31 with the added challenge of managing premature menopause, which can cause fertility issuesâthough her journey, from ideation to undergoing treatment, took more than a decade to come to fruition. âAfter my divorce, my plan was to do embryo adoption because I was in menopause, so I didnât have any of my own eggs,â Purdie says, referring to the option to acquire an embryo from another couple and carry it herself. âI was just sort of collecting information about all the different options as a single woman and what that [path to motherhood] might look like.â Then she learned of a friend who had frozen her eggs in Greece, and it sparked a lightbulb. After looking into options in Turkey, Greece, and the UK, Purdie settled on the Barbados Fertility Centre not only because of the 50% cost savings compared to the US, but also because of the warmth and compassion of the staff she met during a visit and exploratory phone calls. âThe information and the data, of course, is really important,â Purdie says in reference to the clinic's 72% success rate with donor egg IVF treatments. âBut it's a pregnancy. You're trying to bring a baby into the world. There also has to be kindness, patience, and positivity.â Life took a few more turns for Purdie, and she didn't begin her fertility treatment for 15 more years, though she knew the clinic would be her path forward. By the time she reached Barbados at age 46, she had married her best friend of 12 years and arrived with a new plan: fertilize a donor egg with her husband, instead of adopting an embryo as she'd initially intended. With eight donor eggs shipped from their home state of California, Purdie and her partner achieved two healthy female embryos and were able to transfer one to Purdieâs uterus, allowing her to carry the pregnancy. That first attempt was successful, and Purdieâs daughter turns one this month. âTo become a mother at 47 has been the biggest blessing of my life,â she says. She plans to transfer her second embryo next year at age 49. Inspired by her experience, Purdie now shares her story on social media and runs a community called IVF Sisterhood in hopes of encouraging other women with fertility issues, especially those going through IVF past the age of 45. Though the community isn't exclusively for those looking beyond the US for treatment, there are plenty who are. âFor so long, infertility has carried so much shame and trauma that we just sort of shrink,â Purdie says. âI feel so much joy every single day [since becoming a mother], and I really want that for any woman or family who wants that for themselves.â Cost and quality of care are often cited as the top motivations for medical tourists. For Felicia Garay-Stanton, who works in public relations and fashion marketing in New York, the current political climate in the US, including the rollback of womenâs reproductive rights, also played a role in her decision to travel to freeze her eggs at the IVF-Life Madrid clinic. She ultimately conceived her son naturally, four years after her egg freezing in Spain, but Garay-Stanton says that she feels at ease knowing her eggs are stored in a safe place should she need them in the future. âI just like the fact that in Spain they have [legal] protections for all reproductive rights, especially if you're a single female, or if youâre LGBT,â Garay-Stanton says. While Spain allows single women and same-sex couples to seek IVF treatments with a sperm or egg donor, other countries, like the Czech Republic, only offer these services to heterosexual couples, which is important to understand while researching options. The minimum age for an embryo transfer is typically 18 years oldâthe maximum, however, varies more widely, with countries like Greece setting the limit at 54; Barbados doesnât allow transfers past 49. Some countries, including Spain, donât allow you to choose your sperm donor, if that's part of your plan; and othersâlike Germany, Denmark, and the Netherlandsâonly allow pre-transfer genetic testing of embryos when thereâs a high risk of severe disease. Understanding a countryâs legal and even social parameters for reproductive care is key when choosing where to go. In South Korea, for example, itâs not strictly illegal for single women to undergo IVF treatments, but in practice itâs almost impossible to access, as clinics typically require proof that patients are in a heterosexual marriage before every IVF cycle. Itâs a fact that Hellynn Jung and her husband know firsthand. After undergoing a lengthy IVF journey in Seoul, Jung, who was born in South Korea but grew up in the US, now openly shares her experience on social media and offers consultations to women seeking reproductive care, especially overseas. Despite the restrictions, Jung says Korea is an attractive option for straight couples who want to engage with a medical system thatâs fast and efficient. â[The process] is very straightforward. No nonsense, and they're really good too,â she says, noting Korea's technological advancements in the medical field. âSo that's the reason why I went back.â The cost savings in Korea may not be as dramatic for Americans as they are in other countriesâthe average IVF cycle in Seoul costs between $5,000 and $10,000âbut according to Jung, people are also drawn to Korea for the possibility of doing beauty treatments and other medical work while there. âKorea is a hub for anything medical,â she says. No matter where someone chooses to get reproductive care, Jung recommends making the process as lighthearted as possible. After being diagnosed with a diminished ovarian reserve, Jung went through 15 egg retrievals and 5 embryo transfers before eventually giving birth at 43. She knows from experience that staying calm is no easy feat, but she is an avid believer that the less stress you have, the better your chances of success. âThe heavier [this process feels], the more [of a] control freak that you become because you're scared, [and then] the more stress you're going to have, and that's not going to be good for your body,â she says. âIf you're traveling for IVF, make it a relaxing, fun tripâ¦ Make it about an adventure for yourself, where you're exploring different things.â For Jung, that looked like attending Seoul Fashion Week and indulging in the cityâs fine dining scene, while for some of her coaching clients, that meant professional color consultations, beauty treatments, and even weekend trips to Japan. When Garay-Stanton reflects on her experience, she echoes a similar sentiment. Since the egg retrieval process, which is also the first phase of IVF, requires 10 to 14 days of daily, at-home hormone injections and doctor visits every few days, there is still plenty of time to explore your destination. âI was going to the appointments, I was doing my shots, but during the day, I could just walk around the city,â she says. âWe took a weekend trip to the Canary Islands, and I just brought all of my medication with me. So my mind was off of it, which I think was positive.â What all these women have in common, myself included, is that we wish we had started our journeys sooner. Whether that means early hormone testingâas Jung and Purdie suggestâor simply knowing that going abroad is an option. âThe US has this mentality that we're so much better than everywhere else, and I think this process has really shown me that there could be even better options [outside the country],â Garay-Stanton says. For those who may worry about the judgment of others when making this delicate decision, Purdieâs advice is simple: âBe honest with the path that you want in life and don't let anybody take it away from you. Because I almost did.â

item.title: Yeti Is Making Performance Apparel. Our Rain Jacket Expert Has Thoughts.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy YETI Tensleep Women’s Hooded Down Jacket YETI Caprock Men’s Merino 250 Quarter-Zip YETI Caprock Women’s Merino 250 Quarter-Zip YETI Sansaba Women’s Fleece 260 Full-Zip Yeti made waves in the outdoor industry last week when the company announced its foray into apparel. This is unexpected, right? Not really. The expansion into outerwear is only surprising if you still consider Yeti “just a cooler brand.” Over the last few years, the cooler kingpin has parlayed its brand recognition and reputation for durability into other outdoor niches, like backpacks. And honestly, they’ve done so with flying colors. Let me start by saying that I am by and large a Yeti fan. Their insulated drinkware has become my go-to for morning coffee. These overengineered insulated bowls have relegated plastic Tupperware to the recycling bin. And then there are the expedition-grade waterproof backpacks, heavy-duty gear-hauling tote bags, these killer gear storage solutions, and more that have all been tested and approved by yours truly and Outside’s team of gear nerds. Hell, this summer, I got my hands on a Yeti carbon-steel wok that can handle electric cooktops and open-flame cooking alike. I was skeptical, but upon first sizzling stir-fry, I was sold. All that to say, Yeti doesn’t just talk the talk. It walks the wok. Cookware humor aside, it’s not remotely surprising to me that Yeti, which goes by the same four-letter ticker on the NYSE, is trying to take a bite out of the massive outdoor apparel pie. But my question is this: Will Yeti’s foray into clothing be as successful as its venture into cast-iron pans, bags and totes, or its ongoing toppling of Tupperware’s microplastic-built empire? The short answer: who knows? Product is limited—insert grumpy emoji here—so we haven’t tested samples yet. When we do, we’ll report back. Regardless, we’ll quickly break down some eyebrow-raising specs and share a few thoughts. Because if we can’t review gear, we’d at least like to gossip about it. The most newsworthy piece of Yeti’s debut apparel line is the Tilloo Rain Jacket, available for $350 in both men’s and women’s versions. But before we get into the numbers that gear nerds care about most (waterproof and breathability ratings), I’d like to quickly tackle price, since I’ve read a few comments from pitchfork-wielding shoppers saying they’d never spend three-hundred-plus bucks on a rain jacket. It’s a fair point, but misguided. Yes, $350 is a lot of money. But it’s closer to average than outrageous for a decent rain jacket these days. Take our coverage of the best men’s rain jackets of 2026, published on Backpacker and last updated in September. When you consider the eight jackets our testers loved the most, the average price is $333. Our favorite do-it-all pick, the Helly Hansen Verglas Infinity Shell 2.0, costs $370. Granted, if you are hunting for an affordable hard shell, you can check out other tester favorites, among them the more than reasonably priced REI Co-op Rainier for a hundred dollars, or the tried-and-true, ultra-durable Patagonia Torrentshell 3L for $189, our top value pick, which gives shoppers the most bang for their buck. Whatever you choose, the $350 price point on the Yeti Tilloo rain jackets is reasonable when stacked up against current competitors. Price notwithstanding, Yeti describes the Tilloo as crafted from a three-layer waterproof, breathable, stretchy nylon fabric. The site doesn’t list a specific waterproof and breathable membrane, like Gore-Tex, suggesting the tech is proprietary. The waterproof rating is listed at 40K millimeters, while the breathability rating is listed at 45K grams per square meter of fabric over a 24-hour period (this rating will often appear as a 40K/45K denotation in product specs). This is where things get interesting. Now, if you pay attention to waterproof and breathability ratings, you already know that these numbers are higher than I was at Golden Gate Park on 4:20 PM, April 20th, during my senior year of high school. (I was violently high.) If you are unfamiliar with these numbers, or you are currently violently high, a quick refresher. The first number references a hydrostatic head test. The exact protocols for these tests vary, but the best way to conceptualize it is to imagine a section of fabric placed beneath a cylinder that’s full of water. You increase the water pressure by raising the water level in the cylinder, and the waterproof rating is determined when the fabric leaks and fails. If the fabric isn’t waterproof, it leaks quickly, resulting in a lower rating. If the fabric is very waterproof, more water pressure is needed, so the rating is higher. The second number refers to a breathability rating that measures the weight of water vapor that can permeate a square meter of fabric in a 24-hour period. The more grams of water that can pass through the fabric, the more breathable the fabric is, and the score is higher. To put this in perspective, we wouldn’t trust a jacket with a 5K waterproof rating in a storm, nor would we do a high-output activity like ski touring in a shell with a 5K breathability rating. In general, the sweet spot is 20K/20K if you’re looking for an extremely waterproof and breathable jacket for a weather-prone sport like skiing. Gore-Tex Pro, for instance, often considered the gold standard waterproof and breathable membrane and the backbone of the Montane Alta XT, our favorite heavy-duty shell, comes in at 28K/25K. With that in mind, Tilloo’s rating of 40K/45K is extremely high. Given what we know so far about this new jacket, are we still curious? Yes. Are we excited? Yes. Are we skeptical? Also yes. These data points are helpful beta, and we always consider them when purchasing a rain jacket. But living and dying by numbers is a fool’s errand. First off, it’s hard to know whether the findings are verified by a third party or provided by the manufacturer. This explains why we test jackets in the field and also send them to the Outside Lab for further side-by-side analysis. What’s more, the fabric itself isn’t always the source of failure for a rain jacket. A rain jacket can score well, only for the taped seams to peel like sunburned skin, the stitching to unravel, or the waterproof zipper to be not-so-waterproof. Additionally, a couple of key numbers are absent from the specs of the Tilloo. First off, we don’t see the fabric’s denier, which quantifies fabric thickness and weight and correlates to durability. We expect Yeti to produce durable gear, but without this data point, that faith is somewhat blind. Even more egregious, weight is missing from the specs entirely. If you’re a discerning outdoor enthusiast using a shell for anything beyond casual, daily wear, that number is critical for your decision-making. Nitpicking and sleuthing aside, the Tilloo does have several features that suggest we will inevitably enjoy it, among them fully taped seams, a waterproof Aquaguard YKK zipper, and a touch of stretch in the fabric itself. One feature that’s missing is pit zips, which we can do without if the Tilloo is as breathable as Yeti claims. After the Tilloo, nothing stands out to me as particularly noteworthy. There’s the Tensleep Hooded Jacket (men’s/women’s), which is Yeti’s take on a classic puffy. It purportedly blends the lightweight, lofty properties of down and the moisture-wicking, anti-odor properties of wool fibers for a hybrid insulator that can handle high-output activities. Again, this sounds intriguing, but with no down fill-power listed (a measure of loftiness that influences a puffy’s warmth-to-weight ratio), no total weight listed, and no opportunity to test, we’re flying blind here. Additional pieces include a variety of mid-layers. There’s a PrimaLoft fleece, plus a full-zip and quarter-zip crafted from NuYarn merino. These are materials that we’ve tested and loved over the years, so we have no reason to believe these Yeti iterations will be anything other than solid. If you’ve stuck with this gear nerd’s meanderings this far, I thank you. I’m also sorry I don’t have more to report. But until we get our hands on this apparel and test it both in the field and at the Outside Lab, it’s tough to say if this is a flop or a triumph. Granted, if I were a betting man, I’d lean toward the latter given Yeti’s track record. If you’re curious or a diehard Yeti loyalist, it certainly could be worth purchasing the new rain jacket or puffy, or checking out the fleeces and merino layers. But if you need a reliable rain jacket that’s co-signed by myself and our experienced test team today, I’d head over to Backpacker to read our men’s and women’s rain jacket reviews. We won’t steer you wrong there. One interesting point that I’ll leave you with is this: some of Yeti’s previous expansions have been made in part via acquisitions. More specifically, they bought renowned bag builder Mystery Ranch in 2024 and cast-iron connoisseur Butter Pat Industries in the same year. As of now, we’ve seen no news of an apparel brand acquisition. It seems like Yeti is breaking trail solo here. But we wouldn’t be shocked to see Yeti snap up a smaller fish sometime in the not-so-distant future. It isn’t “just a cooler brand,” after all.

item.title: The book lover’s guide to literary London
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Hello, my name is Rebecca and Iâm a book addict. I love reading books, listening to podcasts about books, piling books high on my bedside table, and discussing books with friends. My interest in literature is one of the reasons why I first moved to London: I wanted to be in the place where so many of my favourite writers lived and wrote their masterpieces. At any one time, I might be walking past the house that inspired J.M. Barrie in Peter Pan, or where Jane Austen came to stay when she visited London. Thankfully, Iâm not alone, and there are endless places for book-lovers like me to congregate in the capital â not just Daunt Books or the British Library, but a multitude of bookish coffee shops, literary bars and storied pubs that once played host to the likes of Charles Dickens. To say that Iâm in likeminded company would be an understatement. So without further ado, these are the 11 best places for bookworms to shop and socialise in the capital. The book loverâs guide to literary London Best for: the cool crowd, book and cocktail in hand The brainchild of Jonah Freud (current beau of Lily Allen), Reference Point has been dubbed the sexiest library-slash-bookshop in London, thanks in large part to the addition of â youâve guessed it â a fully-stocked bar. Opened at the beginning of 2026, it specialises in visual literature, with a collection of 10,000 photobooks and magazines to peruse at your leisure, and so far has attracted the likes of everyone, from fashion students to a curious Austin Butler. If youâre looking to recreate your meet-cute fantasy of bumping into your true love while browsing the shelves, then this is probably where youâll do it. Address: 2 Arundel St, Temple, London WC2R 3DA The Drawing Room at the BFI Bar, Southbank Best for: an intimate drink amongst vintage books Secrets doors and hidden rooms are a mainstay of horror fiction, yet thereâs nothing scary about The Drawing Room at the BFI Bar. Once youâre inside, youâll find floor-to-ceiling bookshelves piled high with vintage books, which are more for admiring than actually reading. With a menu of cocktails named after films (this is the BFI, after all) itâs perfect for anyone wanting to discuss the latest book-to-screen adaptation. Best for: oenophiles who want to chat about their latest read A place where you can wax lyrical over your love of the latest literature, glass of wine in hand? Thatâs the premise behind BookBar, a wine bar-slash-book-shop that has outposts in both Chelsea and Islington. As well asÂ a roster of regular events, including author Q&As, thereâs also a book club that you can join. Each month, members are sent the book to read, and after discussing it with their peers are also treated to a virtual interview with the author, too. Address: 166 Blackstock Rd, London N5 1HA; 11 Chelsea Manor St, London SW3 3TW Best for: retracing famous writers' favourite hangouts No end of famous writers have enjoyed a pint at The Spaniardâs Inn in Hampstead, including Robert Louis Stevenson, Lord Byron and Mary Shelley. Bram Stoker was inspired by local folklore and ghost stories at the pub in his novel Dracula, while Charles Dickens was a regular and included it in his novel The Pickwick Papers. John Keats even reportedly wrote his landmark poem, Ode to a Nightingale, in the pubâs garden. Best for: book lovers who want one of the world's best drinks Lined with over a thousand antiquarian books (hand-selected by a Portobello antique dealer, no less), Scarfes Bar was designed to look and feel like an old gentlemanâs club. Named after the famous cartoonist Gerald Scarfe, his work lines the walls, giving it less of an imposing feeling. Indeed, itâs somewhere that you can come for a heated debate about the merits of Austen vs Bronte, without drawing too much attention to yourself. Address: 252 High Holborn, London WC1V 7EN Best for: whiling away a whole afternoon Rustique has been luring bibliophiles to north London since 2000, with its distinctive independent neighbourhood charm. Punters are welcome to sit and read for as long as they wish, with no pressure from staff to order another coffee or move on. The menu is no-frills comfort: think jacket potatoes, quiche and soup of the day. In the summer thereâs a small garden with chairs and tables to retreat into as well. Hatchards has an unmatchable pedigree: first opened in 1797, itâs the UKâs oldest bookshop and has no less than two Royal Warrants. As such, its staff are amongst the most passionate book-lovers youâre likely to find, brimming full of enthusiasm for hunting down that rare first-edition signed tome that youâre desperate to get your hands on. Itâs full of literary history too: the desk where Oscar Wilde once signed his books is still here, while Virginia Woolfâs character, Mrs Dalloway, browses its windows in her most famous novel. Best for: a Dickensian London experience Fans of Charles Dickens will want to seek out this hundreds-year-old pub, which is the only surviving galleried coaching inn in London. Thatâs because not only did he frequent it, but it is also name-checked in his novels Little Dorrit and Our Mutual Friend. A stoneâs throw from Shakespeareâs Globe, itâs thought that the Bard and his contemporaries were also regular patrons here too â he even mentions it in his play, King John. Address: 77 Borough High St, London SE1 1NH Website: nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/london/george-inn Best for: a brilliant meal before you read There are multiple reasons as to why Quo Vadis feels like a particularly literary spot. Firstly, Karl Marx wrote his famous treatise, Das Kapital, from here. Secondly, itâs become a kind of meeting place for journalists and authors working in Soho since it first opened back in the 1920s. And thirdly, itâs got a Library Bar, a space specifically designed with reading, drinking and talking in mind. Address: 26â29 Dean Street, London W1D 3LL

item.title: How to Plan an Epic Winter Hiking Trip In France On a Shoestring
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
The French Alps are a year-round cornucopia of outdoor adventures, but until last winter, I divided seasons into separate camps. Winter was for skiing and summer for hiking, with no crossover. But skiing gets expensive, and my dogs can’t come with me, so I racked up even higher costs paying for pet sitters. One of the reasons I love hiking is because it’s one of the cheapest, most accessible, and most pet-friendly sports out there. In winter, it requires a little more investment, but after learning how to tap into France’s extensive system of backcountry huts (AKA refuges), that investment is now largely time rather than splashing cash on technical ski gear and resort vacations. France has over 3,300 refuges, but only around 300 of them are staffed. Here’s a rough-and-ready guide to using both kinds and lining up winter hiking adventures in the French Alps on a shoestring. Many of France’s staffed refuges open only in summer, and those that open in winter are generally on ski-touring or mountaineering routes, which can make them hard for winter hikers to reach. The FFCAM lists manned refuges, with a toggle function to show those open in winter, and how long it typically takes to reach them on foot. A night in a dormitory bed on a half-board basis usually costs $56-$90 (€50-80) per person, or $23-$45 (€20-40) per person for bed-only. State any dietary requirements when you book; meals are generally a one-pot affair. Most unstaffed huts are completely free to use or very cheap, though the accommodations aren’t opulent. The website Refuges.info lists around 3,000 unstaffed refuges in France (cabanes non gardées), and some in other central and western European countries too. The site is completely user-run, which means that if no one has visited a hut recently, information on conditions can be pretty limited. Some unstaffed refuges are so basic that a public toilet would look luxurious. Others have views people would pay millions for. There’s no booking system, so they’re on a first-come, first-served basis. Try to arrive at smaller refuges early. If it’s full when you get there, you’ll either have to curl up for the night on a croissant-sized patch of floor or make a hasty scuttle back to civilization. Not all unstaffed huts have water. There’s a toggle on Refuges.info to filter huts with water sources, but in winter I simply boil snow on the gas stove. Since my winter adventures are generally one or two nights over a weekend, I go a lot more gourmet for food than I would on a summer thru-hike. This is France, after all, so I like to take cheese and make a fondue. Porridge is great for a warming breakfast. If you want to take the easy route, dehydrated meals are also a light and fast way to make dinner or breakfast. Unless you’ve got very technical cold weather gear, it’s a good idea to choose a refuge where you can build a fire, as unmanned refuges aren’t heated. Annoyingly, there is no search toggle on Refuges.info that allows users to filter by huts that have a wood burner or chimney. Instead, search for the area you want, and then click through the descriptions of each hut. Look for poêle (wood burner) or cheminée (fireplace) in the text. Adapt your intended distance and elevation gain to winter conditions. Gaining 3,000 feet of elevation in a day poses no problem to experienced hikers in summer, but very few people could cover that kind of ground in winter. Don’t underestimate how much more tiring it is to walk through snow, and how much shorter daylight is. Personally, I drop down to 600-1,000 feet of elevation gain for winter hikes. Each person or party should adjust to their own skill and experience levels. As with any kind of winter activity, avoid avalanche zones on your hike. It doesn’t hurt to have an avalanche safety course under your belt if you’re adventuring in avalanche-prone terrain. Quite glamorous for an unstaffed refuge, with bunk beds to sleep eight, a wood-burning stove and a large table, flanked by a dramatic limestone cliff. It’s a snowshoe hike of around 90 minutes from St Andéol (7 miles there-and-back). A tiny hut amidst the trees with a fireplace and space for two to three people to sleep on wooden benches. It’s a little over an hour’s walk from La Pesse (5 miles there-and-back). Not only does this refuge have incredible mountain views, but there are 24 bunk beds, a wood-burning stove, and even real toilets—positively luxurious. The trail climbs steeply from Lanslevillard; allow for three to four hours of hiking (7 miles there-and-back). As Refuge de Cuchet is in a national park, no dogs are allowed, and there’s an honor-system charge of about $5.50 (€5) to pay online. Bring what you need to start a fire, and take a gas stove to make yourself a hot meal after a long day outside in the snow. What you bring to start the fire depends on preference and skill level, but I like to bring both firestarters and a lighter. If you’ve got a Nalgene, you can fill it with boiling water and use it as a hot water bottle heater at night. You’ll need a sleeping mat and a sleeping bag for sub-zero conditions (recommended R value of 5 or higher). Insulated snow boots are better than hiking boots, and depending on snow depth, take snowshoes or microspikes. Snowshoes are best in deep snow; microspikes are good for icy patches or hardpack. Pretty much every French town offering downhill, Nordic, or cross-country skiing will also rent snowshoes, usually for around $11 (€10) or so. It gets dark early in the mountains in winter, so bring a headlamp and a fully charged power bank. Most smartphones lose their charge faster in cold weather; store them inside your jacket for better battery life. Dry socks and sliders for the evening are a good idea as unstaffed refuges aren’t always particularly clean. It can also be nice to have a set of warm, comfortable, clean hut clothes to change into after hiking. And of course, always bring a paper map and a compass in case technology lets you down. Staying in an unstaffed refuge in winter is a unique adventure you can plan without blowing your rent for the year. It might not be the most luxurious night of your life, but these mountain huts can be cozy, and they offer access to some really amazing alpine terrain. It’s well worth sacrificing some creature comforts to make the first snowy footprints on the trail in the morning.

item.title: My favourite villa: I celebrated a milestone birthday at this 'White Lotus'-worthy Thai hideaway with Mandarin Oriental service
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
I’m soaking up the morning sun in the pool when a circular basket holding a picture-perfect breakfast spread is placed in the water and gently nudged in my direction. The floating breakfast is a popular trope of hotels in the Maldives and around the Med, but I’m neither in those locales, nor am I in a hotel. My four friends and I are in Phuket, celebrating our collective 40th birthdays at Villa Amarisa, a member of the Mandarin Oriental exceptional homes collection. Among its properties are standout holiday homes in Italy, France, Spain, Greece, Croatia, the UK, Indonesia and another in Thailand. Carved into a cliffside of Kamala, often referred to as Phuket’s millionaire mile, Villa Amarisa comprises three floors with a discreet entrance and top-floor lobby filled with art and hand-carved Indian pillars. From there, the glass house unfolds below with stairs and a lift connecting each level. There are a total of five bedrooms, all with ensuite. I stayed in the ground floor Topaz suite, one of two primary bedrooms, with a sliding door that opens up onto the infinity pool, a wet room on one side of the bathroom and a private terrace with outdoor clawfoot tub on the other. Neighbouring the ground floor suite is a glassed-walled gym. On the second level is the Coral primary suite. The bed is flanked by gold sculptural lamps and there's a private section on the terrace that overlooks the pool, again with a claw-foot outdoor tub. The Lapiz suite was the most zen of all the rooms, with a raised Japanese-inspired tatami bed, a wall of framed bird artwork and views of the lush Kamala cliffs. While we stayed at the villa as a group of friends sans children, it's perfectly set up for families – the Amethyst suite has twin beds that would be great for kids. All come together on the lower level, where a sweeping open plan entertaining space includes a kitchen (a chef’s kitchen sits behind it), TV area with an extended cream chaise sofa, dining area and an elegant sitting area surrounded by wood paneling and curated art collected from all around the world. Rare antiques and original artworks are found throughout the space – wandering down the second-floor hallway is reminiscent of an art gallery. My favourite piece was the spectacular 2,000-year-old apsara sculpture, perfectly placed in front of a large picture window overlooking lush greenery. Even the lift feels distinct – an intricate Indian wooden door frames it on the ground floor. But the biggest masterpiece of all is the 24-metre blue stone infinity pool which, from the right angle, appears to melt into the Andaman Sea and sky. This is where our breakfast drifted towards us, under the shade of a soaring Yang Na Yai tree, and suppers of pomelo salads, freshly prepared lobster and sticky mango rice were served alfresco. The talented private chef Aoy even went to the local market early in the morning to secure a gluten-free soy sauce for one of my friends. In addition to a private chef, the villa comes with the kind of daily housekeeping you'd expect in a Mandarin Oriental hotel, including a turndown service with bedside Ferrero Rocher chocolates. On hand 24/7 was the villa manager Bella, who prepared our morning coffees, arranged any taxis we needed and served us tropical cocktails well into the evening. The best aperitivo took place at sunset on the sprawling rooftop, where an angel wing sculpture – the villa's name ‘Amarisa’ means ‘blessing from heaven' – acted as the ultimate metaphor.

item.title: My favourite Airbnb: I stayed in a converted stable in Cornwall, a surfer's paradise with stargazing from bed
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
It’s not often the British forecast promises dreamy surf conditions and sunshine on a weekend in October, so as I strapped the boards to the roof of the car and cruised down the M5 from London to Falmouth in Cornwall, I felt excited about the days ahead. Things only got better when I arrived at my Airbnb. Here lay off-street parking – don’t laugh. Anyone who has driven to Cornwall before will know the fight for a spot on the road, and I felt like I’d found treasure when I discovered a private space big enough to unload my 9ft board and bags. Morlanow is a one-bedroom former stable and store building, intelligently redesigned by local architect Nina Jones and her partner Alex. It has a curious, sculptural, rounded exterior, which is exactly what stopped me in my tracks mid-scroll during my initial Airbnb search. Inside, the coastal theme is clever as opposed to nautical. The design is inspired by the way boats work, fitted with built-in furniture that doubles as storage, so there’s plenty of room to stow everything a surfer might need for a weekend. It’s compact, but doesn’t feel small. Every inch has purpose without feeling overly engineered. Aesthetically, it’s playful but ‘cool’. Vibrant flashes of colour contradict tactile, natural finishes and pale-wood walls. The front door opens to the kitchen and an open-plan dining area with a wetroom-style bathroom conveniently tucked to the left. There’s a collection of books and a cute little reading nook with a comfy sofa, and the bed is nestled upstairs beneath an incredible skylight window – we had an epic view of the stars from here one night. Mornings quickly developed their own ritual. I’d wake feeling rested as light poured in through the windows, then head out for strong coffee (Dark Pony’s morning brew became a favourite) before flicking through the local surf-cams – a live update of wave-heights and sea conditions with a spotlight on the south coast – and debating which stretch of coastline looked best to beeline for. Mostly, we headed north towards Perranporth and Hayle, chasing down the cleanest conditions we could find. The waves were glassy and punchy, with barely any wind. I surfed until exhaustion hit, promising myself that each wave would be the last for much longer than intended. Coming back to Morlanow after a day like this was when I appreciated the smart design the most. There was somewhere to store boards and space to hang wetsuits, not to mention a much-needed hot shower. When I wasn’t bobbing about in the ocean, I wandered Falmouth, browsing new kit, replenishing my supply of surf-wax, and trying on clothes at Roma Surf Shop, Sessions and my favourite – Finisterre. I found a cold pint of Lightbulb Ale by local Verdant Brewery at the Sea View Inn just across the road from our digs, and enjoyed a cosy dinner further into town at the Seafood Bar. Here, I filled up on moreish Fish Tacos, and a generous plate of fresh Crab Loaded chips – more than enough to convince me that Falmouth takes its seafood seriously. By the end of the trip, my car was covered in sand, my hair was full of salt and my mind was overflowing with ideas about how I could redesign my own home in London. Morlanow was the perfect base for a long, surfer’s weekend, but more than that, a reminder that smaller spaces don’t have to feel like a compromise.
